I want to ask tbe hon. minister whether he intends to prosecute an inquiry into those alleged frauds.

Last year when this question was put to me, I answered it as the hon. gentleman has stated, and I thought the matter would rest there ; but on further representations made by the hon. gentleman, I promised him that an investigation would take place. Accordingly I appointed a person to investigate into these charges of fraud and I hope to have his report pretty soon.
Do I understand that a person has been appointed to prosecute an inquiry ?
Yes, I will bring down the information and give my hon. friend the name and instructions and everything.

I think that is what the hon. minister should do, in view of the fact that those gentlemen who made those allegations are supposed to be inplicated in some personal matters in that connection and in order also to give the fishery guardian charged with these frauds an opportunity of vindicating himself before a proper representative of the government. I think the matter very important and trust the inquiry will be prosecuted without delay.

I want to call tlie attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to a campaign sheet issued by his department giving a review of the improvements in the lighthouse and coast service of Canada between 1896 and the 30th of December, 1903. It is a new departure that any minister should have a campaign document published in connection with his department. The hon. gentleman shakes his head, but this is nothing else. I know of no greater outrage than for a minister to use his position and department and the public funds for the purpose of publishing and disseminating campaign literature. The hon. gentleman may find precedents, but po matter where he may have selected his models, what he has done is not in the public interest.

When I got an official of the department to prepare this statement, it was in order to inform people on the other side of what he was doing for the St. Lawrence route. In doing this, I simply followed the example of my predecessor who issued a similar pamphlet. The information in this pamphlet is taken from the report of the Marine Department. It is a condensation of what is contained in that report and better adapted for ready reference. The hon. gentleman would be surprised if I were to show him the numerous letters we have received from England and other European countries asking for more of these pamphlets, so as to post themselves on what is going on in the department. We at first ordered 2,000, and these were distributed only to people connected with the shipping interest and members of parliament.
It is very fortunate perhaps that some members of parliament got them on this side.
They were sent to every member of parliament.
I am not questioning that statement. The pamphlet purports to be a review of the progress and development of the Department of Marine since 1896. Why was that date selected ?

It is after 1896 that the most important work was done. In 1894-5-6, there were great complaints against the St. Lawrence route and we had any amount of difficulty in dispelling the wrong impression that had been formed regarding it. We all know the efforts that were made by the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal and the shipping interests of Quebec and Montreal in 1896 to convince the government that it was a question of life or death for the St. Lawrence route that certain improvements should be made ; and it has been since that time that large sums were voted in order to improve the route and remove the bad impression which had been formed concerning it.

Of course, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Prefontaine) is always single-Mr. HAGGART.
minded in everything. It was by the merest accident that he selected the year 1896 for comparison. The hon. gentleman devotes his whole effort to show that there was complaint in 1895 or 1896. Has he been asleep that he does not know that these complaints had been made for years before and have been made for years since ? The charge was made by one of his own supporters, the hon. member for St. Lawrence Division, Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike), from his place in the House that the whole service was in the most deplorable condition. Why did not the hon. gentleman (Mr. Prefontaine) date it from that time ? He could hardly have been ignorant of the complaints that were made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bickerdike). But, in compiling this table to show what has been done on the St. Lawrence route he, incidentally and quite accidentally, fell upon the year 1896. I do not mind giving the hon. gentleman my opinion that that is mere parish politics and looks all the worse when practised by the head of a great department. The hon. gentleman brought action against a newspaper for having stated more definitely, not than the facts warranted, probably, but than he was willing to have known, that he had established a sort of bureau in his own city through which his friends would secure places, it appears that it is a part of the outfit of the government to which he belongs. The Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) on one occasion when he was acting Minister of Public Works, advertised for applicants from one end of this country to the other-
That is entirely without foundation.
I will take occasion to refresh the hon. gentleman's memory.
Do so, if you can.

I will do so with pleasure, and probably with not a little pain to the hon. gentleman. Evidently the hon. gentleman has forgotten. It is said that reckless people never take pains to remember what they have said. I would not say that the Postmaster General was reckless, but he was new in the business and anxious to distinguish himself. So, when the back of the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal (Mr. Tarte) was turned, he resolved to out do that hon. gentleman and learn every place that wanted a wharf or a dodk. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries-
I hope the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) will not omit the proof. He was going to give the proof of his statment. Will he not make good his word ?

If the hon. gentleman (Sir William Mulock) will allow me a little time, I will call the witnesses-including himself. Now, returning to this pamphlet,

let me review some of its features. It purports to give a * comparative statement of total expenditure for the fiscal years 1896 and 1903. ' This includes items for ocean and river service, lighthouse and coast service, scientific institutions-was there any complaint about that ? Marine hospitals, steamboat inspection-was there a controversy about that so keen that people were crying out for information about it for the year 1896 especially ?-and civil government salaries.
What has all that got to do w'ith the improvement of the St. Lawrence route ?

Perhaps the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will tell us that. How much are the people of the old country concerned about civil government salaries ? Were they thirsting for information with regard to steamboat inspection ? Did they demand to be informed about our scientific institutions ? Then we have a comparative statement of the expenditure for lighthouse and coast service for the years 1896 and 1993. The first item is for salaries and allowances. I am sure the people abroad were anxious about that. And so it goes through with the other items. It is, no doubt, a very complete campaign document. I congratulate the hon. gentleman on the efficiency of the work from that point of view. Let me read the italics on page 5, put there, no doubt, by direction of the hon. minister himself-for I will venture to say he took great care in the preparation of this pamphlet :
Since the year 1896 one hundred and fifty-six towers and inclosed lighthouses have been built and fifty pole lights have been erected, making a total of two hundred and six new lights put in operation.
Why was that put in italics ? I will sit down and await the hon. gentleman's explanation.
To call the attention of the reader to the statement, I suppose.

The reader would not have taken notice of it, if it had not been put In italics, I suppose. Had they put in the name of the hon. gentleman himself, it would have been a more direct way of accomplishing his purpose. The public are not so dull as to require the italicizing of important statements by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Here is another statement in special type : Will the hon. gentleman say that the public were so much interested in this that he needed to call special attention to it ?
Lighthouses to be put in operation next spring and others for which tenders have been invited.
Was that given prominence so that people might come to the hon. gentleman and
look for contracts ? The hon. gentleman assents to that. I am glad he is so frank. Then there is a comparison of the number of lights in the Dominion of Canada for the years 1896 and 1903. I shall not trouble the committee to go more in detail through this interesting volume of thirty-two pages, including index, of campaign literature. I would advise the hon. gentleman, however, as a fitting frontispiece to put on the front of the cover his own photograph looking as wise as he now tries to look after having issued this splendid campaign sheet.
I shall carefully consider that advice.

It seems strange that the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) should have any doubt concerning the motives of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in choosing the year 1896 as the year with which comparisons are to be made in this pamphlet. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) looking after the interests of the Militia Department and Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prefontaine) looking after his own department go back to 1896 for comparison, and prepare campaign documents to be circulated as public reports. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prefontaine) had a reputation before he came here, and this is simply what we expected from him. A dozen of these pamphlets were sent to each member of the House, and every member was invited to send for as many as he pleased for distribution. But, owing to the nature of the pamphlet, I did not send out so many as I would have been glad to do otherwise. The fact that the comparisons are made with the year 1896 shows that it was intended to be a campaign document and so I did not care to send them out.

I am afraid the hon. gentleman will have to wait until the Committee on Public Accounts sends for the vouchers, or gets an explanation why there are no vouchers. I certainly do not come here charged with explanations for vouchers for the employment of every cabman. All I can say about that is that I cannot afford to keep a horse, I am too old to walk, and as long as I hold my position, I think the hon. gentleman will have to submit to paying my cab fare.
'Now the late Minister of Justice, the Hon. David Mills, had this to say about it :
I cannot say that I agree with the hon. gentleman that there should be no objection to cab-hire for the First Minister simply because he is the First Minister. That is wholly a new doctrine. 1 always supposed there was a sessional allowance granted to every member of this House, granted to the Prime Minister as well as to others, and he may use a portion of that sessional allowance to pay for his Mr. TAYLOR.
cab-hire precisely as he may use it for any other matter. If the House is of opinion that a different rule should be applied to the First Minister, the House ought to proceed regularly. There is no authority for the premier, any more than for any other member of this House, to come to the House in a cab and charge the cab-hire in the public accounts. He has no special position in that respect.
Mr. Mills is an authority for the doctrine that no cabinet minister has a right, any more than any private member of this House, to charge for cab-hire. This was the charge against Sir John A. Macdonald, and he was the only man of the government! against whom Mr. Mills could bring a charge of making the country pay for his cab-hire. But look at the list now. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has in this account before us, for a portion of last year, a charge for cab-hire of $53.50, and for travelling expenses of $437. Why does not the same rule apply to him that Mr. Mills laid down for Sir John A. Macdonald? The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has his sessional indemnity, and he should put his hand in his own pocket and pay for his cab-hire. There is no law allowing him to charge these accounts to the country. Here is the highest authority stating that the Prime Minister, the late Sir John A. Macdonald, had no business to charge for cab-hire. In the ' Hansard ' of 1889 you will find that the opposition spent hours criticising the late Sir John A. Macdonald with having misappropriated the funds of this country in charging for cab-hire. My hon. friend who has just stepped into the government cannot go down the street without calling a cab and sending the bill to the government. I certainly think that this ought to be put a stop to some way. If each of the cabinet ministers is going to have a bill of from $400 to $600 every year for cab-hire the government should introduce a bill authorizing them to do so legally because we have the statement of the late Mr. Mills, who was the Minister of Justice in this government, that it is contrary to law, that no cabinet minister has any more right to do this than any other member of the House. I would like the hon. gentleman to show me what authority he has for placing in the public accounts cab-hire to the amount of $53.50 for a portion of the year 1903-4 ?
The same authority that existed in the time of Sir John Macdonald.

speechtext: Mr. Mills says there is no authority for it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
By the First Minister only. Some hon. gentlemen say there should be

an exception in favour of the First Minister and so there should be. I will never by act or voice object to any charge made by the First Minister for cab-hire or for travelling expenses. With the exception of the hon. Minister of Customs every one of the ministers is guilty. This never was done by the late Conservative government as it is being done by this government notwithstanding the fact that the late Mr. Mills said it was contrary to law. I want the hon. gentleman to explain where he finds the authority, either by law or practice for any such charge being made except by the Prime Minister of Canada.

No doubt if it had been illegal the Auditor General would not have passed it.
Mr. TAYLOR, I submit that is an unsatisfactory explanation. I beg to move :
That the Item he reduced by the sum of $53.50, being the cab-hire charged by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries as shown in the Auditor General's Report of last year.

Before the vote is taken on this question I desire to say that there is a principle involved in this extending far beyond the amount that is named by my hon. friend from South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) who has just moved the reduction of the item. The principle is far reaching because what would apply to this department would apply to all the departments of government, and there is no doubt that this practice of charging up to the country Items of personal expense by ministers which to my mind have no connection whatever with the department is a growing evil and is becoming a somewhat cumbersome matter to the country. I think it is time we had some understanding and that if the government desire to continue this practice which in bygone years they denounced as being wrong they ought to place some law on the statute book authorizing it and making it clear that they have the right to take this money out of the public treasury and apply it for their personal benefit. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries has offered, to my mind, a very flimsy excuse indeed. He savs that because it was allowed to the late Sir John Macdonald it ought to be allowed to all the ministers who have succeeded him. Sir John Macdonald said that he was old, that he could not afford to keep a horse, and that so long as the country required his services he thought they would be obliged to pay his cab-hire. I do not think the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries will come down and make any such confession as that. He cannot say that he is too old to walk. I do not think that after the successful career he had in the municipal council of the city of Montreal and with the reputation he achieved, he will claim that he is too poor, and I think therefore that some better excuse should be offered
than that which the hon. gentleman has offered for the charge that is here made. It you can apply it to cab-hire of course you can apply it to street car fare. We find that this is a growing item. More than that, you can apply it to the use of private cars, which, by the way, is becoming rather a serious charge. Although it is indirectly that the country pays for them there is no doubt that all these private cars, whether they go to Mexico, or wherever they go, are all paid for by the people of this country. It is done by exchange, an exchange which this country has to make good to the American roads when they desire it so that practically we are paying for all these junketing expeditions of the government whether on street cars, in cabs, or in private cars.
I think it is time that some principle was laid down and that the people should know whether or not ministers have the right more than any other member of parliament to place their hands upon the public funds without the authority of law and appropriate them to their own personal benefit. I do not think it is a healthy state of affairs and it seems to me that it leads step by step along the line which eventually will bring about a very much more serious condition. I hope the hon. minister for his own sake will be able to offer some better justification for the taking of this money and applying it to his own private purposes than he has yet offered. I desire to say in reference to this pamphlet as it has been printed by the order of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that the same courtesy should have been extended to every member of parliament and that it should have been sent to every member.
It has been.
I have not received a copy of it. I made careful inquiry in the post office and there was nothing there. I do not see why it should be given to one and not the other.

I persist in affirming that instructions were given when the pamphlet was issued in January, 1904, that copies should be sent to every member of parliament. I have no reason to doubt that the instructions were followed but I will inquire.
Will the hon. minister send us some now ?
With pleasure.
I would like very much if the hon. minister would send me a copy.

time. They take particular care that the comparison shall be between the years 1895 and 1903. The foundation has been falling into decay for a number of years and at the present time it will hardly support the structure. It looks dingy. I want the minister to tell me why it is that the fishing bounties have fallen off considerable since 1895 and 1896? I put a question on the order paper the other day, asking why the bounty was not paid to the lobster fishermen, and in the usual manner I was put off by being referred to the law on the question. That answer was neither a sufficient nor a fair answer, when I asked for the reason why the lobster fishermen did not share in the bounties the same as other fishermen. Let the minister now tell me why the policy is followed, by which the lobster fishermen are not included in the bounty. ?

From the Auditor General's Report of 1896 I find that the Hon. Geo. E. Foster was paid $120.75 for cab-hire. What is the use of saying that cab-hire was only paid to the Prime Min ister of the Conservative government, when we find that the other ministers drew cab-hire just the same ?
Your friends said it was wrong.

Never mind what my friends said. Speaking about campaign literature ; gentlemen opposite had better turn their attention to the kind of campaign literature they are circulating throughout the country. It reflects no credit upon themselves or on anybody else.

That is a question of judgment, and I cannot commend the hon. gen tleman's judgment. I want to get from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries an explanation as to what extent his department has been enlarged by the recent changes.
I find that one year J. Thompson drew $251.25 and C. H. Tupper $119.25 for cab-hire. This shows that the other Conservative ministers drew cab-hire as well as Sir John Macdonald.

When the Liberals were in opposition they condemned Conservatives for drawing cab-hire ; and if they are consistent, why do they themselves now draw large amounts for cab-hire ? Surely the hon. member for Victoria is not so dense that he cannot see the difference.
ROSiS (Victoria). I am not so dense as the hon. gentleman thinks, but I have shown here that other ministers of the Conservative government, as well as the Prime Minister, drew cab-hire.
No person contended anything different.

The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) stated repeatedly that only Sir John Macdonald drew cab-hire, and not the other ministers.
Mr. SPROUiLE. What the member for Leeds said was that he would have no objection to the First Minister drawing cab-hire, but as the Liberals condemned it the other ministers should not draw cab-hire. The gravamen of the charge is that the highest authority in the Reform party, the Hon. David Mills, declared in ftiis House that there was no legal authority for the First Minister or anybody else drawing money for cab-hire. The hon. member from Victoria (Mr. Ross) was a member of the Mackenzie cabinet with the Hon. David Mills, and he must know very well that if it was wrong then to draw cab-hire it fs wrong now, because the law has not been changed since. The trouble with these gentlemen over there is that what they condemn in their opponents they justify when it is done by themselves.
The cab-hire drawn by the Minister of Marine was objected to, and the statement was made that only Sir John Macdonald drew cab-hire when the Conservatives were in power.
No.
Is it right or wrong for the men now forming the cabinet to denounce this when they were in opposition and to practise it when they came to power? That is the point we are dealing with.
Let our conscientious friend from Victoria (Mr. Ross) answer that question.
It strikes me that it is right always for a cabinet minister to engage a cab when it will facilitate public business.
Is it right for your friends to denounce it when they were in opposition and to do the same thing themselves when in power ?
It is always right if it advances the public interest.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Rossi did not understand what I

read from ' Hansard.' I will read some more of the debate in order to enlighten him :

Judging from the way 'this account is made out, I should say this country, on a small scale at all events, is being humbugged by our Barnum minister-
That is the way he described the late lamented Sir John .Macdonald.
-as much as the United States people are being humbugged by their Barnum. If the hon. the First Minister can be in two places at once, the people ought to know it. That this year there has been expended $728.15 for cab-hire for persons not named in the vouchers is ta, matter that requires as much explanation as this account. Therefore I cordially agree with the hon. member for Bast pigin (Mr. Wilson) that this requires some explanation, and I can.see from the happy mood in which the First Minister appears to be that he is just in the vein to explain it. I would be glad, for my own satisfaction and that of the people, if he would be kind enough to rise in his place and tell us how it is that he can by any possibility be riding in a cab at Ottawa while travelling in the car ' Jamaica ' and making political speeches in Toronto, Welland and other places.
Then Sir John Macdonald replied and was followed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright), who last year, according to the Auditor General's Report, spent $300 for travelling expenses- I suppose to Hot Springs-and $496 for cab-hire ; and yet he was one of the parties who attacked the late Sir John Macdonald, then Prime Minister, for having employed a cab. Every member of this government except the Minister of Customs has a bill for cab-hire ; and some day we will perhaps divide the House on that matter. My hon. friend from Victoria, N.S. (Hon. Wm. Ross) certainly did not hear what X read as the opinion of the late Minister of Justice, the Hon. David Mills, who ought to be an authority for him and an example for every hon. gentleman on that side of the House to-day. If the Prime Minister of the Conservative government did spend some money for cab-hire, certainly this government, which is pure and just and upright, should not put their hands into the people's pockets and take money for cab-hire which the late Minister of Justice (Hon. David Mills) said should come out of their own pockets. Here is his opinion of it :
I cannot say I agree with the hon. gentleman that there should be no objection to cab-hire for the First Minister simply because he is the First Minister. That is wholly a new doctrine. I always supposed there was a sessional allowance granted to every member of this House, granted to the Prime Minister as well as to others, and he may use a portion of that sessional allowance to pay for his cab-hire precisely as he may use it for any other matter. If the House is of opinion that a different rule should be applied to the First Minister, the House ought to proceed regularly. There is no authority for the premier, any more than for
any other member of this House, to come to the House in a cab and charge the cab-hire in the public accounts. He has no special position in that respect. My friend the hon. member for East York (Mr. Mackenzie) is a member of this House and was at one time the Prime Minister. He had devolving upon him the important duties now devolving upon the First Minister. In consequnce of his assiduous application to those duties, he is scarcely able to get to his seat in this House, yet I do not find that the right hon. gentleman has made any provision to bring my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Mackenzie) here in a cab.
There is the opinion of the late Minister of Justice, the legal authority of the Liberal party of Canada, discussing the matter with reference only to the Prime Minister. No other minister was mentioned in the whole debate which then took place. It was an attack upon the Barnum of Canada, as they called the late-lamented Sir John A. Macdonald-that was the respect they paid to him-a man who did more to build up Canada and make it a nation than all those men frut together who sit on that side of the House. These gentlemen were not too small to attack him and charge him with having mis-appropriated the public money, because he came to the House and went from the House at midnight in a cab. Poor old man, who died at a ripe old age, without a dollar in his pocket, after having governed this country for many years 1 The poor old man said :
' I am too old to walk, and too poor to buy a horse'; and yet these gentlemen attacked him and charged him with having misappropriated the people's money. When these purists came into powrer, they said :	'We
are going to do business on business principles and in an honest way ' ; and yet every minister except the Minister of Customs charges his cab-hire to the people of this country. That is what I condemn. According to the Auditor General's Report, these hon. gentlemen spent in the year 1902-3 no less than $203,399.18 in travelling expenses, railways fares, cab-hire, tips and sundries-just for six departments. The ministers spent for travelling expenses $7,477.84, for fares $475.92, for cab-hire $1,061.10, and for sundries $45.60. The Labour Department spent for travelling expenses $3,891.55. The Justice Department spent for travelling expenses $4,658.42, and for cab-hire $116.33. The Marine and Fisheries Department spent for travelling expenses $8,473.85, and for cab-hire $58.60. The Department of Militia and Defence spent for travelling expenses $7,842.22, and for cab-hire $139.44. The Inland Revenue Department spent for travelling expenses $27.07, and for cab-hire $33.75. The Department of Indian Affairs spent for travelling expenses $827.71, for cab-hire $365.95, and for tips $39.90. The Department of Agriculture spent for travelling expenses $28,055.23.
How many years does that cover-fifty ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It covers one year, according to the Auditor General's Report.
That is not correct. The hon. gentleman is mistaken.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will name a day when he is going into his estimates, I will give him the figures. I will give them to him now if he likes.
Giye them to me now- the travelling expenses of the Minister of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am not saying the minister. I am saying the department.
Oh. That is another business.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman spent for travelling expenses in connection with his department $28,055.23 and for cab-hire $854.73, for tips $2, and for sundries-I do not know what they are-peVhaps this was aii for lemonade-$562.23. The Interior Department spent for travelling expenses $52,811.49, for fares $473.95, for cab-hire $4,097.05, and for sundries $99.27. The Public Works Department spent for travelling expenses $58,238.73, and for cab-hire $512.65. I have not worked out the details for the Department of Finance, Customs, Secretary of State, Railways and Canals, Privy Council, Printing and Stationery, Post Office, Mounted Police and Trade and Commerce ; but these seven departments which I have mentioned spent $203,399.18 of the people's money for travelling expenses in order that these gentlemen and their civil servants might go around the country ; and they spent in tips and sundries nearly $1,000-I suppose for lemonade and so forth. And yet, after reading what the late Hon. David Mills said, what authority have they for doing it ? There it is, nearly a quarter of a million of money. No wonder they want the revenue to flow in to keep up this state, of affairs. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, though only a few months in office previous to the 1st of July, 1903, and though he is a young man and as able to walk as anybody, spent for cab-hire $58.60. That is the way the people's money is being wasted and then we are refused any information. The only reply we are given is that the other fellows did it and we are going to do it too.

I do not wish to take any credit not due to me. If there is no cab-hire charged against me, I suppose it is because my secretary paid it and included it in his travelling expenses. When I go on official business, I frequently hire a cab in order to keep my appointments ; and if cab-hire is not charged against me, it must be because it is charged in my private secretary's bill.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We are talking of cab-hire here in Ottawa. Cab-hire out of Ottawa would be included in travelling expenses.

I very well remember the late Sir John Macdonald being criticised for spending money in cab-hire, and his reply was that he was too old to walk and too poor to afford to keep a horse, and that as long as he remained in the position he had, he was afraid the country would have to pay his cab-hire ; but I am astonished that the hon. member from Victoria (Mr. Wm. Ross) an old Baldwin Reformer should plead that because the late government charged up cab-hire for the premier, the present government was justified in doing the same thing for the whole crowd. But as he and his party condenmed the late government, they are not justified in making the plea they do. Will the hon. gentleman tell me that when he appears before the great judge of us all, he will venture to plead that although he condemned certain things done by the late government, the present government are justified in doing the same thing because their predecessors set them the example. Is that the kind of reform doctrine we ought to expect from an old Baldwin Liberal ? You would think that these hon. gentlemen would be ashamed to do the same thing which they condemned in their predecessors, and not only that but spend hundreds of dollars more in the same way. Why, we have ministers now who cannot go down to a summer resort without a special car. We have a minister who, when he came to Ottawa, was well known not to be very rich, but where is he to-day ? He is living in a palatial residence in this city which cost him $20,000. He bought Corby's yacht, which was too expensive for Corby to run, and all the silver plate in it, and all that could not have cost less than $20,000 more. He cannot plead, as the late Sir John Macdonald did, that he is too old to walk and too poor to keep a horse, because he does keep a horse. I am not so penurious as to object to paying cab-hire of ministers, but what I object to is ministers getting into power under false pretenses and then doing exactly the same thing as their predecessors did, and pleading that as valid excuse I say they are doubly guilty.

I am afraid that the advice we are getting to-day was not very palatable to hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in office, because all this cab-hire and travelling expenses went on then as now. [DOT]	,	[DOT]
Not one-half as much.
Not only did the ministers then charge for cab-hire but in many cases their deputies were paid their cab-hire as well.
And you said it was wrong.
E-QSS (Victoria). I did not.
But your party did and you are responsible.
1 am only responsible for what I say myself and not for what my party do. I find that the travelling expenses of Sir John Thompson amounted to $1,486.67.
That is not eab-hlre. Mr. WM. ROSS (Victoria). Cab-hire at Ottawa $251.25
The Minister of Trade and Commerce spent nearly $500.

Hon. gentlemen opposite talk about the Department of Agriculture. Well, I have just looked up the Auditor General's report and I find that that department was charged with cab-hire to the extent of $32. I take the hon. gentleman's statement that it was in Ottawa. I do not know, but I can say that on no occasion have I ever had cab-hire charged the government except when on government business, such as taking distinguished strangers out to the experimental farm.

I wish to say a word about this celebrated pamphlet for which we are to pay. It is a reminder of ' Political pointers.' The Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) laughs. He would not have regarded it in the same way had this been perpetrated by his political opponents when he was on this side of the House. It may be that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prefontaine) has an ambition to fulfil the highest expectations of his leader the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), as set out in this celebrated Order in Council which has been laid before us. As the doctrine laid down is a new one, and as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries seems to believe in it and tries to carry it out, it seems worth while to call attention to it. This Order in Council says :
In the case of members of the cabinet, while all have an equal degree of responsibility in a constitutional sense, yet, In the practical working out of responsible government in a country of such vast extent as Canada, it is found necessary to attach a special responsibility to each minister for the public affairs of the provincial district with which he has close political connection.
I take it that the district with which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has such close political connection as to justify his getting out this pamphlet is the St. Lawrence route, and so he orders the preparation of this pamphlet by one of his subordinates and calls upon us to vote the money to pay for it.
Mr. Fisher, while sharing with his colleagues that general responsibility already referred to, represents in a particular manner the eastern townships of the province of Quebec.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries represents in a particular manner the St. Lawrence route, I suppose, and it is, of course, proper in accordance with that principle, that he should get out some special report informing the world of what has been done in that locality under his charge. I presume he justifies this pamphlet on these lines. I wish to say a word also about the item mentioned by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor). That hon. gentleman takes exception to the expenditure of $90 for dictionaries for that department. As the ordinary dictionary costs about fifty cents, I suppose we may take this expenditure to mean that the department has bought 180 dictionaries. I would criticise this more severely were it not for the fact that some members of the cabinet cannot distinguish between a Scotchman and a ' foreigner.' I think dictionaries are needed by hon. gentlemen opposite in the interest of the country, and the more dictionaries they use the better. It may prevent the Minister of Marine and Fisheries falling into some such blunder, and the more he avoids such things the more it will be to his credit.
With regard to the item of travelling expenses, these expenses do not seem to end with travelling expenses. You have here cab-hire, tips, sundries, even payments for accident life insurance. We find the charge of $53 for tips for a single trip. These people are very liberal with what does not belong to them. We are told that Artemus Ward was willing to sacrifice all his wife's relations to the cause of the Union. These people seem to be quite ready to make themselves appear big men with the country's money. That reminds me of a story that is told about the great maritime province politiean, Joseph Howe. One disagreeable night he reached a cozy hotel, where he found everything very comfortable. He found excellent stabling for his horse, and, while ordering a drink in the bar he complimented the landlady upon the way in which her hotel was managed. He threw down a five dollar gold piece. When she offered change, he refused to take it, but said, 'We will talk about that in the morning.' He was given a very nice supper. On this also he complimented the landlady, and, ordering another drink threw down another five dollar gold piece, again refusing to take change-saying that he was busy and did not want to trouble about that, that they would make it all right next day. The landlady was surprised and could not make out what kind of a man this was. The following morning he again complimented the landlady, telling her that he had had a splendid night's rest and a fine breakfast, and again threw down a five dollar gold piece, but still would not hear of receiving change. The landlady said, ' Who are you, any way ? I would like to know

what kind of man you are.' ' Oh,' he said, ' We make our money easier that you do.' This does not cost me anything. I am the Honourable Joseph Howe and have access to the public treasury. Money does not cost me anything.' ' Well,' answered the landlady, ' I always knew that a Grit would steal, but I never knew before that he would give it away so liberally when he got it. Whether these gentlemen steal it or not, they seem ter be quite willing to give it away liberally. Take the case of one subordinate officer, Mr. Frank Pedley.whom I have met many a time on the platform- a very genial, good natured soul. There is a charge from him of $233.04 for travelling expenses, including $75.25 for pullmans, and $35.25 for tips. Whether he has stolen it or not, he has become possessed of it in some way and he seems to be willing to give it away as easily as Joseph Howe. Now, I object to this because it sets an exceedingly bad example to the rising generation. It is the duty of the government to deal as economically with what belongs to the country as they would with their own funds. But, as long as the government regard it as proper to hand out public money in tips, travelling expenses, cab-hire, buying trunks for themselves, paying for accident insurance, and so on, we shall not have the economy exercised anywhere in the public service that we ought to have.

Hon. members on this side are not opposed to reasonable expenditure for cab-hire for the ministers. What) we do object to is the statement by these hon. gentlemen before they came into power that, if given office they would abolish these things which they complained of as abuses before 1896. So far as I am concerned, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) for instance, has never been found fault with though he is carrying out a system that these hon. gentlemen condemned before 1896. He has been a long time in the service of the country, and has been unfortunate in the matter of health, and- I, for one, would be sorry to object to any reasonable expenditure he'may incur for cab-hire . The same would apply to the leader of the government and any other minister. If our party came into power, we would expect to spend reasonable sums in the same way, and I think the country should be willing to pay. But what we object to is that they are doing now that which they declared to be wrong and their only justification is that we, when in power did the same thing. I bave a quotation in my hands of a speech made by a present minister of the Crown previous to 1896. Speaking to the electors in a certain part of the Dominion, he said :
You have the right to hold the politician to his pledge, just as much as you would the man of business.

The man who obtains goods from you under false pretenses is a cheat and swindler.
What should you call the men who obtain votes by means of pledges which they never intended to keep ?
I say again, if you are prepared to overlook these things then you have no right to ask for fidelity from any man who hereafter represents you.
Sir, it was the present Minister of Finance who said that. I know hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House do not deny that they have broken their pledges. They have no principles, they do not pretend to have any principles ; they are simply opportunists, and they take advantage of the public feeling in the country at the moment, regardless of whether it is in the interest of the country or not. They have violated every principle they claimed to hold up to the present moment, and for that reason I am justified in saying that they have no principle other than the principle of remaining in power. I remember distinctly in the matter of private cars when Conservative ministers were condemned for going from place to place in private cars. I am ready to say, as a member of the opposition, that I think a minister is justified in using a private car if it is in the interest of the country that he should do so in order to transact public business more expeditiously. If the Conservative party came into power to-morrow, I should be prepared to defend the government in a reasonable use of private cars. But as I said before, we are not now finding fault so much with the hon. gentlemen opposite for using private cars as we are for doing the same thing which they condemned the previous government for doing previous to 1896, and they are now afraid to stand up and admit that they were wrong then. Now with respect to the item we are discussing,
I would ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to explain in what way his department has been enlarged, and what branch he has taken over from any other department.

A few moments ago,
I put some questions to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, to which I would like to get a reply, it was regarding the fishing bounty. I see in this campaign pamphlet-
Do I understand the minister declines to answer my question ?

I cannot answer two questions at the same time. I will try to answer one after the other. The hon gentleman has asked me why the amount paid for fishing bounties ha's diminished. Well, in the report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries for 1903. I find the following remarks made by the Commissioner of Fisheries :
During the year 1902 -the fishermen of the maritime provinces received the Sum of $159,853 as fisheries bounties on their respective catches

of deep sea fish for that season. The owners and crews of 795 vessels received $71,079 of the above amount, while the balance, $88,774, was distributed amongst 20,229 boat fishermen. To cover these amounts, 12,723 claims were paid ; 91 were refused payment as being fraudulent. For the last season Nova Scotia received nearly double the amount of bounty distributed to all the other provinces, amounting to $100,455 ; Quebec received $36,125 ; New Brunswick, $14,555, and Prince Edward Island, $8,716. Since its inception (1882) the sum of $3,315,966 has been distributed among ithe fishermen of the above-mentioned provinces to improve the development of their sea fisheries. The regulations governing the payment of such fishing bounties, as well as full particulars respecting their distribution, will be found in appendix number 2.
The same amount is always voted every year, but the amount distributed varies according to the catches. In 1901 the catches were the most numerous. As to the causes of the variations they depend on many circumstances. Sometimes the fishing season begins later and sometimes the weather is unusually stormy and various causes which cannot be controlled.
Would the minister tell me why this bounty is not given to the lobster fishing ?
Because they are not included by the law. The fishing bounty is only paid to deep sea fishermen.

Would it not be well that the boat fishermen should participate in these bounties also ? The lobster fishermen are boat fishermen, and I cannot understand why they should not be paid also. I would invite the minister to bring this matter up in council and see if some relief cannot be given to these fishermen. I see no reason why they should be prevented from participating in these funds, while other boat fishermen throughout the maritime provinces do participate in them. The minister has shown a difference between the bounty paid in 1895 and that paid in 1896, saying that the catch was larger in one year. Well, I am aware of several cases where that principle has not been followed out. For instance, the lobster and oyster fisheries have been falling off simply because the service has not been sufficiently protected. 1 gave an instance the other day where the minister had departed from the Order in Council, refusing the grant of any new licenses and some new lobster canneries had got licenses in a place where the circumstances wiere absolutely at variance with the policy announced by the minister in that regard. Now, I find :
Of the many efforts made by the Dominion government to foster and promote the sea fisheries, the most recent, and in many respects, the most remarkable, is that of providing, under federal auspices, facilities for the storage and preservation of bait in refrigerators. The subject of cold storage for bait, and of fishery products generally, has for over twenty years engaged the attention of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
He goes on to laud the policy of the present administration in regard to the bait grievance. Now about a month ago a newspaper was sent to me from a party down in Nova Scotia, giving some information about the bait freezers, and it would seem from this letter I find in the paper, that the bait freezers are not the unqualified success the minister would have us to understand. For the benefit of the minister, I will read this clipping, dated May 5, this year, and the committee also might like to hear it :

They are not the success which their promoters said they would be.
Although much has been said about what the Canadian government has been doing to enable fishing vessels to procure bait, scores of vessels are now in the harbour waiting for that article.
This was on May 5th of this year :
The Fisheries Department of the Canadian government has tackled the problem of a full and constant supply of bait in a manner at once inefficient and extravagant. Its actions in this connection have obviously been dictated by a desire to advance the interests of party rather than to promote the welfare of our fishermen. This is admitted, and regretted by all interested in the fisheries, irrespective of their political allegiance. Even Moses Nickerson, -who was one of the first to advocate government encouragement to a cold storage system, has condemned the department's methods of establishing bait freezers on the coast.
As a number of fish merchants have for some years been operating bait freezers for their own purposes, the proper procedure would have been to hold out inducements to these men to extend their operations in this line, and to give a bonus not on the construction of freezers, but according to the amount of bait placed in them. This was the method advocate.i by practically all authorities on fishery matters.
The government, however, could not see its way to encouraging fish merchants to increase a legitimate line of business-probably because some of the more prominent men owning and operating bait freezers were not of the right political complexion. So it paid half the cost of twenty-four small bait freezers, which for very natural reasons have been of no practical benefit to the fishermen. The companies organized to take advantage of the government's bounty had no experience with cold storage plants and consequently some little error in construction or operation militated against their success. In one instance, a freezer was insulated with ordinary tar paper, and the bait and food fish placed therein became so impregnated with the odour of tar as to be completely spoiled, whereupon the officers of this particular company wrote to the Fisheries Department that they had lost $500 or so by the experiment, and that if the government did not make good their loss it would lose some valuable supporters in that constituency. A naive confession, doubtless, of the political creed of the ' Laurier and Prd-fontaine ' Grits !

Not content with wasting $25,000 or more on the small freezers, the government has made arrangemnets to bonus the construction of a large freezer in Canso-to expend $30,000 or $40,000 to no purpose, except possibly to help its machine workers. The Canso Cold Storage Company, which will receive this government grant, proposes to supply the bank fleet with frozen bait. The prospectus of the company should be read by all fishing vessel owners and by all fishermen. "With easy indifference to the rights of our fishermen, it shows how the franchise for $31,000, granted by the government to the Whitmans of Canso, to be exercised for the benefit of the bank fishermen, is to be converted into an instrument to promote the interests of a group of capitalists.
As matters stand at present, the hopes of the company, as foreshadowed by the prospectus, are not likely to dispose of 10,000 barrels of frozen squid to the bank fleet every season, and make a profit of $5 on every barrel. Our bank fishermen will buy squid direct from the catchers rather than from this company, because, while fresh and unfrozen squid will keep in their holds a week or more, bait taken out of cold storage decomposes in a few hours. The establishment of a large bait freezer at Canso cannot therefore, under present conditions, be of much benefit to our bank fishermen, though the promoters of this project will doubtless be well paid for their trouble by the government grant. In devising its latest cold storage scheme the department has ignored a factor necessary to success- that is the fitting of bank fishing vessels with cold storage plants. With a large supply of frozen bait at ports like Canso, fishing vessels provided with cold storage could utilize frozen bait effectively, and could carry on their operations with much less loss of time than now. These plants could be put in for $35 or $40 per vessel.
The cold storage plan is all right in principle ; and if worked out in a practical manner would no doubt be of great advantage to the fishermen. But the Department^ of Fisheries is anything but practical, and its efforts in this connection are only likely to increase the difficulties of the fishermen in procuring bait, owing to the fact that the large grant to the Canso Cold Storage Company will tend to enable that concern to acquire a monopoly of that commodity in the vicinity.
It is little wonder that Nova Scotia fish merchants are advocating the Scotch method of administering the fisheries ; that Is, by a board of practical men, representing every branch of the fishing industry. In Scotland the board of fisheries is independent of politics, and is somewhat analogous to school boards in this province. The appointment of all officials under its control is determined by competitive examination, thus insuring the choice of the most experienced and best informed men. In Canada, where the only qualification for office under the department is a political pull, the majority of fishery officers can hardly distinguish one fish from another. As at present constituted, the Fishery Department is an easy mark for politicians, with theories and friends who need the public- money in their business. Witness the work of Dr. Kendall. It was this Mr. LEFURGEY.
politician who initiated the government bait cold storage scheme, and who, not content with wasting $25,000 in small freezers, fathered the scheme to put public money in the poekets of the Whitmans, of Canso. About three years ago Dr. Kendall, at the expense of the government, fitted up a Furness Line steamer with cold storage apparatus in order to test the possibility of shipping fresh lobsters to the United Kingdom. At the government's expense, Dr. Kendall sailed for England with a consignment of lobsters. At the end of three months, after taking a post graduate course in London, the doctor returned to Canada, but though his excursion cost the government about $7,000, nobody seems to know whether or not it demonstrated anything of value to the lobster industry. A Halifax fish merchant informs me that he has repeatedly tried to procure a report of Dr. Kendall's experiment from the Fisheries Department, but without success.
Before the hon. gentleman lays that away, will he kindly give to the committee the name of the author of that document ?
This is a newspaper article taken from the Halifax ' Herald,' and it was sent up to me with the request that I should look into the matter.
Will the hon. gentleman say if the ' Herald ' says so ?

This is headed ' Fishermen's Herald,' and it is taken from the Halifax ' Herald,' and as the Halifax 1 Herald,' like all other good Conservative papers, is working in the interests of the fishermen and of other people in the maritime provinces, I have no doubt it does not publish matters that it is not cognizant of.
Will the hon. gentleman deny that this is the work of an anonymous correspondent ?

Will the hon. member for Cape Breton keep quiet until I am through, and then he can have his say ? Now, in the face of what the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries has put into this pamphlet, X would respectfully submit thar the article I have just read should be taken into the consideration of this House, and that an investigation should be made to ascertain whether this campaign pamphlet is right or whether the case as stated by the correspondent of the Halif ax 1 Herald ' is right. There is no doubt that if the hon. minister cannot account in a better way for the money that is being expended in his department, he will be like the Minister of Agriculture. I understand that one of the cabinet ministers in the corridor last night asked : Well, how did the Minister of Agriculture get along ? The answer was : Oh, Well, he got leave to sit again. I am afraid that if the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries does not give us a better explanation than he has he will have the same

treatment meted, out to him. He will have leave to sit again.

Mr. Chairman, will you permit me one word of explanation in regard to the subject matter before the committee ? The article quoted by the hon gentleman is the work of an anonymous correspondent in the Halifax ' Herald.' I have some knowledge of the situation as regards the fisheries in my own constituency, and all I have to say to the hon. gentleman is that he will not get a reputable fisherman in Nova Scotia to vouch for the statements which he has quoted from an anonymous correspondent in the Halifax ' Herald.'

It does not make any difference in the world whether the correspondent is an anonymous one or'not. If the hon. gentleman wants to turn up the article he can get the Halifax ' Herald ' of May 5th and see it for himself, and I have no doubt that the Halifax ' Herald ' will readily give the correspondent's name. But the main question is not whether this is an anonymous article. An article appearing in the public press in condemnatory terms of the work of the department on this line should certainly be called to the attention of this committee. The main question is whether this article is true or not. In the face of the campaign sheet issued by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and paid for by the people's money, claiming that the government are doing so much in the matter of cold storage for the deep-sea fishermen, it is interesting to read the statements made in this article published in the Halifax ' Herald.' The matter comes down to the question whether the article is true or not, and whether the hon. minister is not misrepresenting, as in the case of the numerous other campaign pamphlets that we find floating around the country.

I would like to ask the Hon. gentleman whether he is prepared to say that any reputable fisherman in Nova 'Scotia is responsible for the article which he has quoted ? It is insulting to the intelligence of this committee for the hon. gentleman to come here with an expression of opinion from a man who is both afraid and ashamed to give the people of this country his name.

I have listened with a great deal of attention to the accusations brought against members of the government for their delinquencies, or rather for taking what does not belong to them according to their own version. What I wish to talk about principally is the condition of the St. Lawrence river, and for which the Minister of Marine is somewhat responsible. Although he has not been long iii office he ought to know something about that river, for I believe he was raised at the head of navigation. It is his duty to see that that river of which we are all so proud should be made so as to be navigable without danger. He is aware that last Sunday morning an accident happened near Lake St. Peter by which a number of valuable lives were lost. I happened to be in Montreal last Sunday, and some of the officers on the Atlantic liners told me that they would not be surprised if many more accidents should take place. It was pointed out to me that nothing but pieces of white board scantlings stuck up in the river, were the guides for navigation. When I came up the river 17 years ago, we had green boughs along Lake St. Peter.
It was Palm Sunday.

Of course that was not under the present ministry, but I do hope that the St. Lawrence river will be put in such a position that vessels will not be subject to be wrecked. It would not have occurred and should not if proper lighthouses were in that river ; so I am told. I may say that it would not cost as much to put electric lights all along down the sides of that river, as would the loss of one of these large steamers. The question discussed this afternoon is whether the members of the government have the right to charge their cab-hire. According to their own showing they have no right, and they have been in power for eight years and have not made a law which would give them that right. Don't let this session pass without making a law under which a man who is working in the interests of this country will not be compelled to walk from station to station, or even from his home if he is an elderly person, without having his cab-hire paid. But let us have it legally done. It is said :
I told you that the gentleman's name was appended to the article. If you want it you can have it, but you appear to be more anxious about the name than the truth of the statement that is made.
Give his name.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the statements are not true.

I say most emphatically they are not true.
He that takes what isn't his'n If he's caught he goes to prison.
These people who take what isn't their own leave themselves open to the law, and the ministers should not be in that position. Let them make a law at once so that a cabinet minister in the discharge of his duty, or deputy minister either, shall be allowed cab-hire legally. But, when it comes to life insurance it seems to me that we poor -I was going to use a strong word-have to insure our own lives, and so should the members of the government. They should

pay their own insurance out of their salaries and not expect the country to pay it for them. And as regads ' tips ; ' if they think that the poor people who pay the taxes feel warm hearted enough let them pay the 'tips' out of their own pockets. I don't think that the poor people who pay the taxes of Canada, should pay ' tips ' for a man who is drawing $7,000 a year. I want this government to make a law now, so that when the independent party comes into power, and that won't be long, we will be able to pay the cab-hire legally. If the government does not make it a law legalizing this cab-hire, the responsibility for wrongful charges rests upon them.

I wish to state to the bon. gentleman that he has been greatly deceived by what has been told him in reference to the accident last Sunday. The facts were misrepresented to him. The St. Lawrence from Sorel to Montreal is the best lighted part of the channel ; there are gas buoys on both sides of the channel, and the accident was entirely due to a mistake by one or the other of the pilots, and had nothing to do with the channel in any shape or way. If we had lights every ten feet it could not prevent an accident when one or the other of the pilots makes a serious if not a criminal blunder. This is not the time, nor the place to discuss this question, because this important investigation, although ordered, has scarcely begun, and will not be finished for some days, until the commissioner can get the witnesses before him, when the ss. ' Cape Breton ' returns from Sydney. I can promise the House that there will be a thorough and complete investigation into this casualty, which I repeat is not due to the river channel, because at that point there is certainly over a mile and a half of channel with from 15 to 40 feet of water. I do not wish the statement to go abroad without being contradicted, that this part of the channel is not in proper condition.
I would be very sorry indeed to say anything that is not strictly correct.

I do not mean to say that the hon. gentleman would make the statement unless it were made to him, but I certainly do think that somebody misrepresented the facts. It is well known to every one that at that part of the channel the aids to navigation are perfect.
Who is responsible for the proper signal lights on a vessel ?

The rule of the road regulates that. I do not want to prejudice the case in any way, but certainly a mistake has been made and the investigation will show who is responsible. The rules of the road were not carried out by some one of the officers.
The minister is quite right in saying that we should not prejudge the case, but it is stated that the accident occurred because of an insufficient signal light. Who is responsible for that ?

The accident must have happened through an error of judgment on the part of one of the officers as to the distance between the two steamers and as to the speeed with which the ' Cape Breton ' was going down. She had just lifted anchor and was steaming down. Probably one or other of the officers did not correctly calculate the swiftness of the current.

I understand that one of the vessels gave the signal to pass by the left, and the other passed to the right, which of course meant a collision, and that one of the vessels blew the whistle a second time to indicate that it was determined to take the left side.
Of course, I will not discuss the matter at present, as it might prejudice the case of one party or the otner. It appears clear that one of the boats was within its rights.
I would like to ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries why the buoys have not been placed in the Napanee river this spring ?

There has been some delay, but they are being placed now. There have been delays in many places this spring owing to the high water and the difficulty of reaching the points where the buoys are usually placed. That is the information I have from the department.

I think there are other reasons. One man has been attending to this business for many years, and he only got $60 for doing it ; and my information is that he has been informed that a vessel is to be sent up to place these buoys. If that is the case, the work cannot be done for double that amount of money. Besides, I think it desirable that the man who attends to them should live in the town of Napanee. I understand that there has been some difficulty with the minister as to the contract for keeping the buoys. I would like to know what the contract means-if it is not for placing them in the spring, looking after them during the summer and taking them out during the fall ?
I will look over the contract and see.

I would like to have all the information in reference to this matter.
I may say that the contract is dated in July, and I understand that the department expected that this man would put the buoys out this spring. He was instructed in April last year to place the buoys, and

the contract would be sent up to him to be signed. I understand that the department expected him to place the buoys In the river this spring as part of the contract, which would be doing a year and a half's work for one year's pay. I would like to know how soon the minister will give me the information.
To-morrow. I will send it to the hon. gentleman by mail.
The minister remarked that the portion of the river from Sorel to Montreal is the best lighted. How many gas buoys are in that distance on each side of the river, and how far are they apart ?
I will lay on the table of the House a chart, showing the position and the number of buoys, with all the explanations.

I presume that the minister is prepared to give some explanation to the House and the country in reference to the pilots and officers generally in travelling up and down the St. Lawrence. The cattle shipped by that route come largely from the province of Ontario, and the freight rates have been very largely increased ; and I presume the minister will be prepared, either now or at some later time, when I intend to bring the matter up more definitely, to explain what is the training and qualification of these pilots, and what system he intends to adopt so that they will know something about the business. They do not seem to know much about it now.

speechtext:
I hope the hon. gentleman will also give a report of the number of lighthouse-keepers on the St. Lawrence whom he has dismissed on one or two months' notice. Some of them have been doing service for fifteen or twenty years. I understand that the hon. gentleman, shortly after assuming office, went into an arrangement for using acetylene gas, that he has large works in Prescott for making the tanks for holding the gas, and a large steamer for delivering them at the points where the lighthouses are, and that this steamer is to move around and look after the lights in place of the men who have been faithful servants for many years, and who have been simply told that their services are dispensed with. I would not object to the change if it were going to effect economy ; but in my opinion it is not, but on the contrary, it will double the expense of every lighthouse on the St. Lawrence west of Montreal. There is the expense of a hundred men employed at Prescott building the tanks, the expense of purchasing carbide, which is made here in Ottawa, and in which one of the ministers, I understand, is a large stock-holder. I do not know whether another of the ministers is interested 1G0
in the works at Prescott, which were formerly in Morrisburg, or not; but the whole thing appears to me to be a big job, while the poor men who have been serving the country for years have been told to go on a month's or two months' notice, and without any retiring allowance except a couple of months added to their salaries. I put a question on the paper some time ago in reference to two men at Gananoque, and the minister replied that they had been fourteen years in the service, that their services had been dispensed with, and that it was not the intention of the government to give them any further remuneration than two or three months' salary. I think that is treating faithful servants unfairly. If it were going to save the country expense and give better lights, there might be some excuse for it; but I do not think it will. I would like the hon. gentleman to bring down a full detailed statement, showing how many employees between Montreal and Toronto have been dispensed with, the number yet in the service, what moneys, if any, have been paid to them, if it is the expectation of the government to make any saving in the annual cost of keeping the lights, and if so, how much, from whom they are purchasing the carbide, and who are the shareholders in the companies that sell the government the carbide and other supplies.

I will not undertake to give a list of the shareholders in private companies. All the other information I will be glad to furnish the hon. gentleman. I may say that the change from coal oil to acetylene gas was Inaugurated by my predecessor on the recommendation of the officer in charge of this part of the department. Up to the present the change has worked very satisfactorily. We will be obliged to cease employing certain lighthouse keepers, but most of these lighthouse keepers complain that they are not paid enough. Most of them are applying every week and month for increases of salary, so that really I do not know that the case is one of very great hardship. There may be hardship in one or two cases, but I have not been made aware' of any special case.

I am not aware of it.
Coming back to the question of bounties, I understand that the money comes from the fishery award.
There is no such thing in the law. The law regarding bounties does not refer to the award. That question is being discussed with regard to a settlement between the provinces and the Dominion.
In looking up ' Hansard,' in the discussion on the appropriation of the interest from this fishery award, Sir Leonard Tilley said that the interest was being paid over in bounties to the fishermen.
I am not denying that, but there is nothing in the law that refers to the fishery award.

He said further that if this money were handed over to the provinces, the Dominion would be under no obligation to pay a bounty to the fishermen.
I understand that the government is con-Mr. TAYLOR.

The fishing bounty is a very important matter to the people of Prince Edward Island. I was a member of this House when this legislation was introduced to pay the fishermen a bounty, and a few days ago, on the 1.3th of June, I find the following question on the order paper ;

1.	On what principle are bounties paid to fishermen in the maritime provinces ?.
2.	Why are not fishermen engaged in the lobster fishery allowed to participate in the bounty, as well as those employed in other branches of this industry ?

The bounties are distributed in accordance with the statute passed in that behalf.
Perhaps the hon. minister will be able to place before the committee the statute on which that bounty is based.
I think it is the statute of 1888. I will send for it.

While waiting for the statute, might I ask the hon. gentleman if there is a steamer employed in planting oysters in the maritime provinces, and is Mr. Kemp, who was formerly in the service of the government, still in the service of the government ? What amount of money did that service cost last year, and what kind of oysters are being propagated ?

I find that the production of oysters in 1895 was valued at $192,000, while in 1901 the production had fallen in value to $173,000-quite a large falling off. This is in the maritime provinces, and I take the figures from a pamphlet Issued by the hon. gentleman. I want to know what this Mr. Kemp is doing, whether he is travelling around the shores of this country in a steamer at the expense of the public without giving any result.

The hon. gentleman will find in the report of the Fisheries Department, page 105, all the information he asks concerning oyster culture and the reason of the falling off. Would the hon. minister say what results have been obtained from oyster culture in the Murray river ?
I am informed they are giving the best results.

About three years ago.

The results are good, as I have stated.

I remember when, some years ago, the oysters were totally exterminated on the Shediac. Can the hon. gentleman say that oysters have increased on the Shediac river, and to what extent? This work was begun on the Shediac ten years ago, and we should have some good results by this time.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me to refer him to page 15 of the report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries for 1903 ? He will find the whole of the statistics concerning the payment of the fishery bounty and showing how the fishery bounty has been paid since 1882 to this day.
iMr LEFURGEY. I am referring to the manner in which the right hon. Prime Minister answered my question. He tola me to refer to the statute.
If the hon. gentleman had looked at the report he would *have seen how the bounty has been paid.
When I ask for information I am supposed to get proper information and proper courtesy from the other sidei of the House.
The hon. gentleman is not supposed to read ?

Well, I only want to be accorded fair treatment and when I ask a question in a proper manner I suppose that proper courtesy shall be shown me m answering that question. I find that there is no statute regulating the payment of this bounty. I can find no Order in Council in this book although the bounties were paid ; but the second paragraph of the Act says :
2. A statement shall be laid before both Houses of parliament within the first twenty-days of next session, of the mode in which the said grant shall have been expended, together with copies of all Orders in Council relating to such grant and expenditure ; and during the same session and each .session thereafter, a statement shall be laid before both houses of parliament, of the mode in which it is proposed to distribute the grant in the ensuing year, and the assent of parliament shall be obtained thereto.
Now, I do not think the government has complied with that law. Did the Department of Marine and Fisheries within twenty days of the opening of parliament lay on the table of the House a statement as Co the mode in which next year's bounty was going to be distributed, as the law requires.
How can I tell beforehand ?
You can make an estimate, the same as you do for the other services of your department and according to this statute you are obliged to do it.
It appears in the departmental report which is laid before the House.

That report tells how last year's money was distributed, but it says nothing about the ensuing year, and you have not complied with the law. I asked the minister why the lobster fishermen did not participate in the bounty, and I got no satisfactory answer. There is nothing in this Act to prevent the lobster fishermen sharing in the bounty the same as other fishermen, and the government can pass an Order in Council at any time to allow them to participate. I strongly urge on behalf of the 1,'obster fishermen of Prince Edward Island that they should get a share in the bounty. The lobster fisheries have not been so lucrative of late years as they formerly were, and those engaged in the industry are entitled to their share of this bounty. There is another question I want to ask the hon. minister. In the event of the Si,500,000 of the fishery award being given t'o the provinces, and when Prince Edward Island gets its share to be utilized probably in wiping off the debt of over three-quarters of a million dollars mcuried bv the extravagance of Liberal administrations, and especially by the present administration during the past ten years ; are the fishermen of the province to continue to receive the bounty ? I asked this question before, and I was Fold by the minister that this had nothing to do with the matter, but I find on page 1512 of Hansard ' for 1882, that when Sir Leonard Tilley was introducing this Act, he stated :
It was also considered that the interest on the $4 500,000 awarded by the Fishery Commission should he distributed among the fishermen who, under its operation, had been compelled to give up the advantage of having access to the American market for their fish. We hope within the next month or so, to he able to pass the Order in Council based upon this resolution to an extent that will very likely he about the $150,000 asked for.
It was the declared intention of the government at that time, that the fishery bounty was to be granted from the interest accruing on that $4,500,000, and now, if that money is to be paid to the provinces,
I would like to have an assurance from the government as to what will be the position of the fishermen with regard to the bounty.

I wish to make a remark or two on the subject brought before the H-'ouse by my hon. friend (Mr. Lefur-gey). I hope his object is not to stir up the fishermen on the island, into believing that the bounty will be done away with. Of course the Minister of Marine does not know until the question is decided by the proper tribunal, whether the Dominion government will have to give this money to the provinces or be allowed to retain it. When that point is settled it will be plenty of time to decide whether the Dominion government shall continue to pay the bounty or not.
Not at all.

The fishermen have the assurance of the premier of Prince Edward Island, that in the event of the money being given t'o the province, and if, the Dominion government does not continue to pay the bounty, then the provincial government will pay the same sum that is now received by the fishermen of the province. That amount will be paid at any rate, and the fishermen are quite satisfied on that score.
We will have to wait and see if they are.
