We will have to wait until the question is decided. This is a question in reference to which legal authorities have held different opinions ever since the fishery award was paid. The late Minister of Justice took strong ground, that the money belonged to the provinces, and Mr. Dickey, who was Minister of Justice ill the Conservative government, also held the same view. The question is open to argument. After it is decided it will be time for the Dominion government to consider whether or not they will continue to pay the bounties to the fishermen. There is one suggestion which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lefur-gey) makes, and in reference to which I am in entire accord with him. I believe strongly that bounties should be paid to the lobster fishermen in certain cases. In the earlier days, the lobster fishermen did not receive bounties because the boats in which they fished were generally owned by the lobster packers, and they made a good deal of money out of the business. However, at the present day a great number of the lobster fishermen own their own boats, and as the lobster fishery is not so remunerative as formerly the bounty would help them a great deal. The suggestion of the hon. member for East Prindfe (Mr. Lefur-gey) is well worthy the consideration of the minister, and especially so when we find that the payments made to the fishermen of Prince Edward Island, as compared with those made to the fishermen of Nova Scotia, are very small indeed. It has been small for the last twenty or thirty years.
I would like the minister to consider that aspect of the matter.

I am not in accord with the remarks of the hon. member for Queen s (Mr. MacKinnon), for I think we are entitled to know what position the fishermen of Prince Edward Island will be in if this distribution of the money should be made. Being somewhat familiar with the financial position of Prince Edward Island, and the obligations we are under already,
I can readily see that if this money is paid over to the provincial government, it will be used to wipe out a matter of $1,000,000 which has already been run up and is in-

creasing at the rate of from $25,000 to $50,000 a year ; and if the fishermen in Prince Edward Island have to depend upon the Liberal administration to carry on the affairs of Prince Edward Island without a deficit, and to leave an amount over for the payment of the bounties which we want extended to the lobster fishermen, they will come out at the' short end of the horn ; and I consider that we have a right to a statement from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries on this occasion as to the exact position this question is in before the government.^ I know that the representatives of the different provinces have been here on three or four occasions, and I have it on very good authority that an arbitration is1 to be held to decide the share to which each province is entitled. The hon. minister) shakes his head. Would he be good enough, then, without my plying him with questions, to make a statement as to what stage this matter has reached ?
There is no statement to be made, because nothing has been done yet.
Does the hon. minister state positively that nothing has been done between the premiers of the different provinces ?
There have been negotiations, but no conclusions have been arrrived at.

I have seen it stated in a Prince Edward Island newspaper that the premier of that province, Mr. Peters, on his return from Ottawa a few days ago, made the statement that the matter" was to be submitted to the Privy Council for adjudication, and that in the event of the Privy Council deciding that the fishery award was the property of the provinces, an arbitration would be held to apportion it. Has the matter gone that far ? What has^ been done in that respect ?
Negotiations have been pending since 1899, I think, but no conclusion has been arrived at.	(
I may say to the hon. minister that the premier of Prince Edward Island, when he was up here the last time, told me that arrangements had been completed for the settlement of this question.
I suppose he knew.

Will the hon. minister tell me, then, what position the bounty would be in, in the event of the disitribu-tion of this money to the provinces ? Is the hon. minister prepared to state that the taking of this money out of the hands of the Dominion government would not annul the payment of the bounties to the fishermen ?
I am not prepared, as I stated just now, to make any statement whatever until the matter is settled or agreed upon.
I am glad the hon. minister has withdrawn from the position which he took before six o'clock. At that time he seemed to be quite sure that this bounty would be paid to the fishermen anyhow.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I did not state anything of the sort. He probably misunder-i stood my bad English. Another time, when I have to make a statement, I will make it in French, and I shall probably be understood.
I understood the hon. minister in English very well.

I have a distant recollection of the discussions which took place over this fishing bounty several years ago. The question was whether the money would be divided among the different provinces according to what each was entitled to, or would be funded and the interest on it paid out to the fishermen from year to year. The contention was set up that if the money were divided, it would be disposed of just as the hon. member says it is intended to dispose of it in the future. It was decided, after long conferences, that it was better to retain it in one fund, and distribute the interest by way of bounty to the fishermen, from year to year, and I think a statute was passed carrying out that intention. Therefore, I take it that no change can be made until that Act is repealed, or until the courts decide that the money should be given to the provinces separately. .

Speaking on behalf of the province of Nova Scotia, I may say that it is not desirous of making any change, but is quite satisfied with the system of bounty given to the fishermen at the present time. I am cer-ainly in favour of the bounty being extended to the lobster fishermen, and I do not see any valid reason why that should not be done.

I can endorse the remarks of my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Wm. Ross) as far as they have gone, but with regaj-d to what my hon. friend fr-'om Grey (Mr. Sproule) has said, while he has some knowledge of the subject, I regret that he has not that accurate and extended information we would desire.
I do not pretend to be accurate!, 'because I was speaking from memory.

The hon. gentleman was in the House representing the county
he now represents at the time that legislation was passed, and I remember right well the then Minister of Finance, Sir Leonard Tilley, being strongly urged by myself and .'others to give this bounty to fishermen because they had become so numerous that their business was not sufficiently remunerative and in consequence were migrating to the United States. We urged that, in order to prevent this, they should be encouraged to prosecute the deep sea fishing and the government of that day acceded to our representations. It was also considered that the giving of a bounty would not only so encourage the prosecution of deep sea fishing, but also the industry of shipbuilding and in this way keep a large number of our mechanics at home as well. But while I endorse the views of my hon. friend from Victoria, I am of the opinion that the government should increase the bounty and give the lobster fishermen a share in it also. These fishermen (the deep seamen) are not getting the reward from their industry which they used to enjoy in the past, and the result has been that many of them have gone to the United States to seek for labour in other avocations. To counteract that tendency, I think the government should increase the bounty and include the lobster fishermen among those entitled to share in it. I understand that the amount of $4,500,000 was in the exchequer of this Dominion for some time before any action was taken to give our fishermen a portion of that money in the shape of interest. It would I believe, be most unwise for this government to hand over that money to the provinces for the reason that in that case it would go into other channels and the fishermen would not have that security with regard to the payment of their bounty which they enjoy at present, whilst the capital sum is funded in the Dominion treasury. I would therefore ask the government to let the matter rest as it is. I was under the impression that it was settled in 1882 with the consent of the respective maritime provinces, I understood that the provinces agreed that this money should remain in the hands of the federal government and not paid over to the provinces, and only the interest on it paid out to the fishermen in the shape of a bounty. I think, now that the fishermen are increasing in numbers, that the amount of the bounty should be increased so that the apportionment meted out to each fisherman would be the same as in years gone by. During the past year the amount was somewhat less than in the previous year.
Not less to boatmen-a little more to boatmen.

The apportionment
was less to the fishermen as a whole than in the previous year. I would strongly urge the Minister of Marine to allow the matter

to rest and not put it in the hands of parties who knew very little about the situation and the needs as respects the fishermen. Let this amount remain where it is and give the increased number of fishermen an increased amount from the exchequer, so that the payment to each man would be the same as in the past and in order that the lobster fishermen might also receive a share in the increased amount of bounty so granted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My lion.'friend is giving us another evidence, of which we have a g'ood many, of the disposition of hon. gentlemen opposite to complain of our expenditures in a general way, and then to argue in favour of increased expenditure whenever we come to details. I am not blaming them on that ground, but I am merely pointing out that when every session they blame us for spending too much, they cannot be very serious. With regard to the lobster fishermen, I think I have stated already that I represent more lobsters in this House than perhaps any member in it. It is a great interest in my constituency, and I should be as anxious as any hon. gentleman to see that the benefits of the bounty are extended to lobster fishermen as well as others. But after all there must have been good reasons some twenty years ago why the grant was not extended to the lobster fishermen. It has never been extended to that branch of the fishing industry and the desirability of doing so was never raised.
It was then held that as the award arose out of our deep sea fisheries, it was the deep sea fishermen who should get the benefit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
At all events, we have had twenty-two years' experience of that system ; and if the payment is to be extended to the lobster fishermen, the resull will be that the amounts to the other fishermen must be reduced. If the expenditure was based, as I believe it was, upon tttfe amount of the award, I fancy it would be difficult to make out a good case for increasing the amount. I am not saying ' No ' to it at this time. I represent a fishing county, and, naturally, I share the desire ot my hon. friend to do the best that is possible for our lobster fishing interest. Still I think it is fair to recognize the fact that the payment was based upon the amount ot the fishery award, and represents the interest upon it; and, while we would have a good case to ask for a reapportionment of the interest, if that were required, we might not so easily be able to make out a case for an increase. I am not passing a judgment upon it now. I would like to see the lobster fishermen of my county, who are numerous, get the benefit, but I recognize the fact that our case would not be so strong now as if it had been taken up in this way Mr. KAULBACH.
twenty-two years ago. To make payments to the lobster fishermen and so reduce the amount to the others might easily cause discontent.

I agree with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) that this was originally given to the deep-sea fishermen. At the time a request was made that the lobster fishermen should receive a share of the bounty also, but that was objected to by those who considered that they had not shared in the sacrifices, to make up for which the award was given by the American government. I would like the Minister of Finance to understand that I do not complain of expenditure when money is applied in the right channel. He can always count upon my support in expenditures when wisely calculated to develop the resources of the Dominion and keep our own people at home in our own country. And the way to retain our own people is to provide that every man shall be able to receive a fair day's wage for a fair day's work. The only way that that can be done in giving a bounty to fishermen is by providing an increased amount in the estimates this year. I cannot see why the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and his colleagues, having the surplus of which they boast, should not be generous enough to meet the reasonable wishes of these hardy sons of toil who earn a livelihood at the risk of their lives on the deep sea, and that by very great exposure and arduous toil.

I am pleased to hear the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) in his little talk on this subject. After his usual fashion, he qualified his remarks before he sat down. He tried to make out that if we gave the lobster fishermen the justice which he believed should be extended to them, we should be taking from the deep-sea fishermen. The statute of 1882 calls for $150.000, which may be expended under Order in Council passed from time to time. This statute does not prevent the government from authorizing, by Order in Council, the payment of money to lobster fishermen, for the matter is entirely in the hands of the government. The hon. Minister of Finance says that for twenty years nothing has been paid to the lobster fishermen. But is that a reason why the lobster fishermen, whose fishery has been decreasing, and who have been earning less money than they did at the time when the statute was passed, should not be now considered ? Is it any reason why they should not have been considered at any time during the last eight years l.on. gentlemen opposite have been in power? As to the plea of the Minister of Finance that if anything is paid to the lobster fishermen there will be less for the others and that dissatisfaction will follow, I find that in 1895-6 the fishing bounty paid out was $163,567, and in 1901-2 the amount whs $159,942.

I think there was an amendment increasing the amount from 8150,000 to $160,000. I know that we always speak of the sum as $160,000.
Mr. LEtFTJRGEY. Then let us have another amendment, Mr. Chairman. In 1895-6 the amount paid was $3,567 over the amount provided for under the amendment of which the hon. minister speaks. As the Minister of Finance feels so strongly that the lobster fishermen should be accorded better treatment, I think he should be able to induce his colleagues to have another amendment and provide for the interest of the lobster fishermen.

I think the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will see that if he grants an increase in the bounty over the block sum of $160,000 per annum the government will receive it back indirectly m another way. There is no class of men in the Dominion who contribute more to the revenue in the way of duties than do the fishermen. When they are successful they live very well, and when they are untoi-tunate and have a shortage in their catch it is pretty difficult for them to get along at all. If the bounty to them is increased, they will contribute as much to the revenue in return, and so the government will not be a loser by the transaction. I urge again very strongly that the hon. gentleman should accede to the request and increase this amount beyond $160,000.
I would like to ask the hon gentleman (Mr. Kaulbach) a question, if I may. Would he advocate an increase to the vessel owners as well as to the fishermen ?

If the revenue will admit of it, I would certainly do so. It would be an encouragement to shipbuilding and to ship owning. I do not wish that to be interpreted, as some .persons attempted to thrust it in my face some time ago when I made a proposition for an increase in this House that it was because I am a shipowner and wanted the benefits Tor myself. I can truthfully say that I would be willing to surrender every dollar of the bounty, so far as I myself am concerned as a shipowner, to benefit the fishermen, but I want to see that the fishermen particularly are cared for. And I say that the increase should be made in a block sum, and let the increase go to the lobster catchers. Then if the government wish to increase the bounty to the deep-sea fishermen beyond what it is at present, I shall be only too happy to see that done also.

The question of the development of our fisheries is one of very great importance.
By an addition to the bounty our fishermen would receive on the average perhaps not more than 50 cents or 75 cents each so this kind of aid does'nt help them much.
But there are some 47,000 of our fishermen who, if they were provided with means to obtain a constant supply of bait, and with better methods of transporting their fresh fish to the markets of the west, would then receive substantial benefit. I do not know what the minister said this afternoon, but I am free to'say that I think the government is dealing with this matter in a broad and comprehensive way. A few years ago I had the honour to recommend to the government a scheme to assist the shore fishermen of the maritime provinces by means of refrigerators, and that scheme has now come into force. 1 would point out the fact that our fishermen have endorsed that scheme to the extent that already some twenty-nine bait refrigerators have been established, and I understand there are applications for five or six more. I venture to predict that before four or five years we will have from 75 to 100 of these on the coast beyond the mouth of the St. Lawrence river. Still these small refrigerators are not sufficient entirely to meet the requirements of the fishermen. According to my idea, and I think it is shared by many others, we should have large mechanical refrigerators at several points in the fishing district, one say at Strait of Oanso, another at Grand Mauan and another at the Magdalen Islands. As a matter of fact if we had had large refrigerators on the coast the summer before last, we could have stored up thousands of tons of bait which would have saved us last year. I think the nember for Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach) will idmit, more than a million and a half ot iollars. Again I say that I think that it the government is going to do anything :o meet the requirements of the fishermen it will not be by giving them small sums of 51 or 50 cents each in the shape of increased bounty. Efficient bait supplies and proper cold storage transportation facilities are the crying needs of the fishermen. While I am ou my feet I would like to say that during the regime of the late Minister of Railways I found it impossible to impress the necessity of furnishing proper cold storage aids for transportation of fresh fish. I must now ask the present Minister of Railways and Canals, and I know I have the sympathy of the Minister of Marine in this matter, that proper refrigerator facilities be provided on the Intercolonial to meet the requirements of the great business that has already begun to develop. Eight or nine years ago the Intercolonial received $9,OUU in freight rates for the transportation of fresh fish, last year it received $27,000 or $28,000, and I think I am well within the maik when I say that it is not at all unlikely that the trade in fresh fish between the east and the west will be developed to such an extent that the Intercolonial will receive uot less than $100,000 yearly in freight.	-

Mr. KAULBiACH. My hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) refers to refrigerators along the Atlantic coast. Last year I endeavoured to encourage the fishermen of my county to invest in refrigerators, and also to encourage a large one in Canso ; but I could not inspire them with the idea that the refrigerator fitted up with a chemical process would be of any service to them. They complained that fish bait frozen for the banks would only remain fresh for a little while, and then become a spongy substance, with no nutritious properties, and the fish only would take that kind of bait when they could not get anythink else. Fishermen as a rule want fresh bait, and when that is not to be had they will then only take bait from a refrigerator.
I am glad my hon. friend has referred to refrigerators, because it gives me an opportunity of speaking of another method that can be employed for curing bait fishes that will be far in advance of the present chemical process. A gentleman named Baton has given me a description of this as a method, which he calls his process. He had an interview with the hon. member for Cape Breton, and I think my hon. friend is possessed with the same idea as myself, that it is an improvement on the old method of bait freezers. Mr. Baton claims that he can make an ice that is completely crystallized and in which there are no air globules at all. He says that air globules in the ice have a tendency to injure or destroy the article intended to be preserved. But there are no air globules at all in the ice he makes, and he claims that it will preserve the fish three times as long as ordinary ice. He also says that it can be furnished for a mere trifle of cost, two cents and a half a ton, and can be made far cheaper by his method than gathering natural formed ice near a refrigerator. He claims that by his process he can make pure ice for domestic use, and that by a current of electricity passing through it all microbes and impurities that are usually found fni water are destroyed. The ice thus produced, he says, is perfectly pure, and will last for a long time. He says that the fish remains fresh and good only so long as it maintains its phospheric properties, and when that is exhausted nothing is left but the pulp, which is not edible either for man or fishes. The same with meat, he says his method will preserve meat for a long time, in fact as long as you might wish to keep it, if maintained at a certain temperature.
I would recommend that the government have an interview with Mr. Eaton in reference to his patent. He is establishing an ice freezer at Montreal another at Toronto and be intends to have one placed in Ottawa. I have recommended him to visit the maritime provinces. He is at the present time in communication with some parties at Halifax and it is to be hoped that they will

grasp the idea as the people in Montreal and Toronto have already done, and that we may soon have an improved system of freezing which will be far in advance of anything that is now employed by the present government at Sydney and other places along the Nova Scotia .shore. I certainly would urge that matter upon the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) who will understand the question sufficiently to see the advantage that would result if an improved system were employed instead of the one now at present under way at Sydney. I would say further that we should have an improved system of transportation which would enable the fishermen of the maritime provinces to get an advanced price for their fish, and that can be brought about by providing a system of cold storage in the cars of the Intercolonial Railway which would enable the fishermen to send their fish right to the Northwest Territories. They can then have all their fish sent summer or winter in refrigerating cars and they can also send boneless fish which, I am glad to say, is now being put up in my own county. There are two industries in my own county putting up boneless fish now in one, two, three and four pound packages which they are placing upon the market. You can take this fish and hold it up to the light and you will see ho bones in it. It is almost transparent and it has not the offensive smell which fish very often have after lying for some little while. If that industry is carried on with proper encouragement and with a bait freezer such as I have spoken of, according to the system of Mr. Eaton, who is the patentee and who has the theoretical as well as the practical knowledge to carry it along, I believe we can make the fishing industry of the maritime provinces equal to that of any that can be found in the way of industries in any part Of North America. I strongly urge again that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries will make arrangements to have an interview with Mr. Eaton and gather from him all the ideas which he has on this subject and which he is quite sure that he will feel satisfied that this new method is in the interest of the fishermen.
I would have brought a practical idea com- -mitted to paper that he gave me had I known that this subject of bait freezers would have come up this evening. I have left it in my room, but at a future time when this subject is up for discussion again I will submit it to the hon. minister or I can hand it to him at any moment.

There has been rather an important allusion made by my hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) to a statement made by the premier of Prince Edward Island, and to a quotation or extract from a paper in Charlottetown as to an agreement being arrived at between the government and the different provinces pro-

viding for a different distribution from that which at present prevails of the amount awarded under the Washington treaty. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries stated that no agreement had been arrived at up to the present moment for the purpose of submitting a case to the Supreme Coourt in order to get its opinion as to the liability of the different provinces.
There are negotiations in progress but there is not final conclusion.

I thought the conclusion was so definite that a request would be made for a special meeting of the Supreme Court for the purpose of obtaining its opinion on this subject. Now that we are discussing the estimates of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, perhaps the hon. minister would state the stage at which these negotiations have arrived and whether the information or current gossip in reference to the matter is correct or not. My hon. friend from East Prince also referred to the distribution of the bounties. I understood that it was statutory, that an Order in Council was to be made for the distribution of bounties from year to year and the principle adopted upon which the distribution was to be made. Has the hon. minister had the Order in Council prepared for the distribution of these bounties in accordance with the statute ?
Certainly. It is passed every year.
It has to be placed oh the table of the House within 20 days after the opening of the session.
It is in the report.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is on the table. It is in the minister's report.
The report is for last year. The Order in Council has to be made antecedent to the distribution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly, that is correct.	-
The Order in Council which is in the report has reference to last year's distribution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But at the time it was passed it had not reference to any past distribution but it had reference to the anticipated distribution. The Order in Council is passed before the distribution is made.

Then I understand the hon. Minister of Finance to state that the Order in Council which was published in the minister's report of last year is the Order in Council intended for the distribution which is to take place of these bounties which the hon. Minister of Marine and fisheries is asking a vote for in the present year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Before we pay the bounty there is an Order in Council passed for the distribution every season. Whether or not the blue-book covers the order for the current year or past year is a point which the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries will have to answer.
But, the point that my hon. friend from East Prince makes is that the Order in Council must be passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can guarantee that it is always passed. It is passed every year before a dollar of the bounty is paid.

The statute *says that the Order in Council shall be passed providing for the distribution of the bounty for the next ensuing year, and that it shall be placed upon the table of the House within twenty days after the opening of the session. Therefore, the Order in Council which the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries referred to was for the distribution of last year's bounty. We are entitled in this House to have the Order in Council that shall be passed showing how this money is going to be distributed for the next year, and I would make one more plea to the hon. minister that the Order in Council this year shall include the lobster fishery.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It cannot do that because the Order in Council for this year is passed.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And therefore the money is being distributed on the basis of that.
That is for last season.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. for the current season's payments. Whether or not the Order in Council for the current season has been brought down I have no knowledge but if it has not been brought down, I agree with the hon. gentleman that it should be brought down. In every case the Order in Council is passed in anticipation of the payment and the money is being distributed now on the basis of that Order in Council. It could not be charged for the present season.
There will be another Order in Council passed at this sitting of the House for next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not passed at the sitting of the House.
During the sitting of the House ?

The Order in Council is passed after the claims are received so that we can base the payment on the claims. The amount to be distributed is $160,000 and the pay-

ment is based upon tbe claims that are received. Before the distribution is made the Order in Council is passed. That is done every year. There are two Orders in Council cited in the report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries of 1903. There is one for 1902 and one for 1903 at pages 10 and 11. That is to show on what basis the payment in 1903 was made. The Order in Council was passed after the claims had been received determining in what way the distribution was to be made. That Order in Council is dated 6th February, 1903. The cheques are being distributed now, and an Order in Council was passed as to what basis the* distribution was made this year. If that has not already been brought down, I will bring it down.
What about the negotiations ?

Negotiations had been pending between this government and the representatives of the different provinces before I was a minister, but no decision had been arrived at. The discussion was as to whether there should be a reference to the Supreme Court to decide the points at issue from their legal aspect, or whether they should be decided on the basis of equity. There was a long discussion on that point, and up to the present it has not been decided whether or not a test case will be submitted to the Supreme Court. If there is a test case submitted, the question arises whether it will be on the legal points, or on points of equity, or whether it will go to arbitration. There is nothing decided.
Just negotiations.

Just preliminary negotiations. A new element has come into the discussion because British Columbia sent a delegate, and we are discussing on what basis we can enter into an arrangement for settlement.

The explanation of the minister is satisfactory so far as it goes ; but it clashes greatly with,' what was said by Premier Peters in Prince Edward Island. I have a statement here given to the ' Patriot ' newspaper by Premier Peters on his return to the island from Ottawa a few days ago.
That is a news-, paper report.
It is from the ' Patriot, ' the organ of the government in Prince Edward Island.
I cannot control that.

Well, here is what it says, and you will see whether it is or not :
The fishery conference.
Premier Peters who returned last night from Ottawa, on being interviewed by * The Patriot ' Mr. PREFONTAINE.
concerning the results of the conference with the members of the Dominion government said that so far as the Halifax fishery award is concerned, it was decided on the suggestion of the Minister of Justice to refer the matter first to the Privy Council of England to determine whether the Dominion government in equity or good conscience should pay . the provinces the share of the award. Should the question be decided by the Privy Council in favour of the provinces receiving the award, the question of the amount payable to each province by the Dominion will be decided by an independent arbitration, to be selected by the provinces and the Dominion. The above course was decided upon, owing to the fact that Nova Scotia could not be persuaded to join with the other provinces in holding an arbitration as at first intended. The matter is being referred to the Privy Council under a statute which authorizes the Dominion government to ask the opinion of the King in Council as to any constitutional' or other matter by which the Dominion government will be bound. This question will, if possible, be submitted immediately to the Privy Council.
At the above conference there were present Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Hon. H. R. Emmerson, Hon. W. S. Fielding, Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick, Minister of Justice, and Deputy Minister New-combe, Premier Peters, Hon. Benjamin Rogers, Hon. George W. Simpson, of Prince Edward Island ; Premier Tweedie and Attorney General Pugsley, of New Brunswick ; Mr. Mc-Ccrkhill, treasurer of Quebec and representing that province ; Mr. A. B. Aylesworth and Mr. G. C. Gibbons, K.C;, of Ontario, who has been retained by the Dominion government. '
Mr. Peters appears to know a great deal more about this than does the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Mr. Peter's statement is in direct contradiction to the statement of the minister and the minister's statement is in direct contradiction of what Mr. Peters said. Mr. Peters states absolutely that there was a conference, and that this was the decision arrived at and he states further :
Aylesworth and Mr. G. C. Gibbons, K.C., of Ontario, have been retained by the Dominion government.
Good jobs.

If Mr. Peters is correct these two eminent lawyers have been retained by the Dominion government, and yet the Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows nothing about it. This is an extraordinary contradiction. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries says he knows nothing about this.

I never said that I did not know anything about the negotiations. The hon. gentleman was out of the chamber, or he did not understand me. I said, there were negotiations, but there was no conclusion arrived at. That is what I said very clearly.
I understand that the bounties which are being paid at present are for 1903 and not for 1904.
Well, of course.
Has the Order in Council* for the payment of bounties for 1904 been passed ?
We pass the Order in Council when we receive the claims.
Then the minister is not complying with the statute.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me to correct him. I have the statute here, and it says :
A statement shall be laid before both Houses of parliament of the mode in which it is proposed to distribute the grant in the ensuing year and the assent of parliament should be obtained thereto.
That can be done any time during the session. The point my hon. friends raised was as to this statement being laid before parliament within the first twenty days of the-session. The hon. gentleman is wrong on that point. What the statute says with reference to the twenty days is :
A statement shall be laid berore both Houses of parliament within the first twenty days of the next session, of the mode in which the said grant shall have been expended, together with all copies of all Orders in Council relating to such grant and expenditure.
That part of the section refers to what has been expended during the past year, and that is complied with by the presenta^ tion of the departmental report which was within the twenty days I presume. The statement as to the ensuing year can be laid before parliament if any hon. member asks for it at any time during the session, and not within twenty days of the opening.
Mr. LEFURGEY; I submit that that d'oes not conflict in any way with miy contention. The statute to which the hon. member for Queen's referred was passed, I believe, in 1886. The statute to which I referred was the firslt Statute. It was passed in 1882, and required that the principle upon which the bounties were to be paid for the ensuing year was to be brought forward by Order in Council, and placed on the table within twenty days after the meeting of parliament. It was not the intention that the detailed statement should be placed before parliament, because that could not come until the number of the fishermen employed and the number of fish caught were known. At the present time we are entitled to call on the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to place on the table a statement of the method by which he intends the bounties of 1904 to be distributed. This is the reason I am bringing up the plea at this time. I am glad that the Finance Minister supports me in the view that the lobster fishermen should receive a portion of the bounty, and, as the Order in Council has not yet been brought down,
I trust that they will be included in the bounty for the present year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As my hon. friend assumes that the statute which he has read is still in operation, I think it would be well to make some inquiry as to that. My impression is that there must have been some amendment to it, because my recollection is that the practice referred to in that statute has not been literally followed.
I have not any recollection of any order being brought down regarding the method of distribution for the ensuing year. Before the discussion is over the minister will be able to ascertain whether there has been an amendment.

I might bring to the notice of the House the fact that in 1891 an amendment was passed providing for the publication of the rules in the ' Gazette ' :
The Governor in Council may, from time to time, make such regulations as he deems necessary or expedient respecting the payment of the said grant and the manner in which applications tor the same or any portion shall be made and established, and may require persons applying for the grant or any portion thereof to verify their claims or any statements made by any person in connection therewith, upon oath ; and any such regulation shall, after publication in the * Canada Gazette,' have the force of law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does that repeal any legislation ?
It does not repeal the Act of 1886, but supersedes it by making other provisions.
The statute of 1886 does not amend the statute of 1882. It is a consolidation of the statute of 1882. It does not repeal sections 3 and 4 of the statute of 1882.
It does not repeal those sections. Anybody in parliament can ask for the statement of the expenditure of the last year and get it, and can also ask for any Order in Council.
That is all the contention we are making. We want to know the principle upon which the payment is to be made, and not the details at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would certainly be very difficult to determine now the manner in which the bounty would be distributed in the next season, because it would be necessary to ascertain the number of fishermen, the number of boats, &c., before the mode of distribution could be determined upon. Of course, if the Act is there, it either ought to be complied with or repealed.

Suppose the minister and all his colleagues advocated the payment of the bounty to the lobster _ fishermen, would not that be a principle of

which the Bouse would be entitled to be informed. I am trusting that the Minister of Finance is going to do this, because he expressed himself so favourably to looking after the lobster fishermen, of whom he claims to have a majority in the maritime provinces. It seems to me that the lobster fishermen should get a portion of this money, and I would like to have an Order in Council brought down giving a bounty to these men.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend's zeal for the lobster fishermen reminds me of a story ; and while it is dangerous to tell a story in parliament, the occasion is sometimes too tempting to be resisted. A man went to a country shop keeper and asked what the price of flour was. Six dollars a barrel was the reply. That is pretty high, said the customer. Well, that is my price, said the dealer. But I have been over at Jones' shop, said the other, and he says the price is five dollars. Why then did you not buy from Jones, asked the dealer ? Because he says he is out of flour. Well, retorted the grocery man, when I am out of flour my price is five dollars too. Hon. gentlemen opposite had many years in which to deal with the lobster question, and they did not do it. I conclude therefore that there must have been very good reasons why they did not.

I have always noticed that the Minister of Finance will contrive to find some little quibble to get him out of a difficulty. He has not advanced any reason. On the contrary he has acknowledged that the lobster fishermen have not received anything for twenty years, and this is the first occasion the matter has been brought up in the House. But the hon. gentleman has been sitting on the front benches during the past eight years, during which time he has not seen fit to bring up the case of the lobster fishermen. But when it is brought up by the opposition, he hurriedly rises in his seat and says some relief should be given them. He will find that he will not be able to dispose of this question by telling a little story, and I trust he will take up the question of lobster fishing in all seriousness. The fact that we have done wrong in the past is no reason why the hon. minister should persist in the same course.
[Mr. FIELDING. The hon. gentleman is mistaken when he says this question was never brought up in parliament before. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule), who has been here for many years, has just told us that the matter was considered years ago, and it was found that the lobster fishermen were not so much concerned in the fishery award as the deep sea fishermen. The reason he gave is fairly open to argument, but the hon. gentleman is mis-
taken when he says this question was never discussed before.
I am quite willing to correct my statement and say that it has not been brought up in this House during the past eight years, during which my hon. friend has been on that side.

The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries would do well to take into his serious consideration the case made out on behalf of the lobster fishermen, especially as he has the assurance that the payment of a bounty to these men will be supported by the opposition. It would be an addition of $100,000 or $150,000 annually to the amount paid at present, and I would ask that the minister would take the matter into his earnest consideration. When hon. members on this side propose an expenditure, they are apt to be charged with extravagance, but in the present instance that charge cannot lie, and I would ask the hon. minister to see whether he cannot come to the relief of these men.

1 rise to endorse' to some extent the remarks made by my hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) but I think he is labouring under a misapprehension to some extent. He divides the fishermen into two classes-the lobster fishermen and the others, but as a rule the same people are engaged in both. If the amount is not to be increased, there will be no practical advantage in giving some of it to the lobster fishermen and some to the others, because in each case the same man would receive in both qualities. I presume there would be some difficulty in the way of increasing the amount. I am inclined to think that our friends from Ontario v. ould oppose any proposition of that kind. I will be very pleased if our Ontario friends would support the government in proposing an additional sum of money to be distributed among the fishermen of the maritime provinces-say $100,000 or $150,000. But I would be very much surprised if they would.
I have often heard them complain that there was too much money expended in the maritime provinces.

Improperly expended.
Mr, J. J. HUGHES. I am glad to learn that they have discovered their mistake and are prepared to vote an additional amount for the fishermen, according to the statement of my hon. friend.
Is the hon. gentleman put up by the ministers to dictate the policy of the government 1
I am speaking for myself only.

If such a proposal were made, would it not be equivalent to an

additional provincial subsidy to the maritime provinces ?
Would my hon. friend support it if it were ?

The amount of the award was capitalized and the interest paid out to the fishermen ; and so long as they get that interest, they are getting all the proceeds. But if an additional amount were voted now, that would be practically an additional provincial subsidy.
'Mr. J. J. HUGHES. That is the proposition which the hon. member for East Prince suggests and which he says the opposition; will support

I never suggested what the opposition would do. I was simply speaking as a private member and stating what I think should be done for the lobster fishermen. I would ask the hon. gentleman from King's (Mr. J. J. Hughes) not to put words into my mouth which I did not utter.

The hon. gentleman said that the suggestion came from the opposition, namely, to pay a bounty to lobster fishermen, but he now withdraws the statement. If the amount cannot be increased, there would be no use in dividing it because the same men are both lobster fishermen and deep sea fishermen. Say the government give four dollars, then one man would get two dollars as a deep sea fishermen and two dollars as a lobster fisherman. That is what the hon. member for East Prince proposes and he thought he was expounding something which would be of great advantage to the lobster fishermen.
Would you support him ?

If this parliament were prepared to increase the amoupt paid the fishermen in the way of bounties, I would support it. I understood from the hon. member for East Prince (Mr. Lefur-gey) that the opposition were going to sup-< port his suggestion.
Nothing of the kind.

I thought as much. And so, the claims of the hon. gentleman and the great sympathy he has expressed for the lobster fishermen of Prince Edward Island fall entirely t'o the ground. I approve very much the suggestion of the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) that the best way to benefit the fishermen is to make provision, as far as is reasonable and practicable, to supply them with bait and facilitate the best methods of catching curing and marketing the fish. I think it is along these lines that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is working. He is fi very practical man and has shown a great interest in the fishing industry.
We have not heard 'of it very much.
You may not have heard of it in Ontario, but we have heard of it.
I suppose the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. J. Hughes) has read the minister's (Mr. Prefontaine's) book ?

Yes, I have seen his work, and I know what the fishermen think of him. And I am sure he will do anything and everything that is practicable to develop the fishing industry and promote the interest of those engaged in it. There is one suggestion I would make to the minister. I- see that, under the regulation a fisherman must catch 2,500 pounds of fish, and fish for three months, to be eligible for the bounty, and that the time spent in fishing lobsters does not count. I would like to see that regulation changed.
That is the crux 'of the situation. That is where the hon. gentleman's (Mr. J. J. Hughes') statements are wrong.
I know as much about this business as does my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey).
You have not shown it yet.

I hope my hon. friend will not continue these unseemly interruptions. They are not creditable to him and are entirely uncalled for. I do not often take up the time of the House, and I am making a statement that, I believe, contains matters that are worth listening to. I believe the regulations should be changed so that the time spent in lobster fishing may count in qualifying for the bounty. The lobster fishermen are the bona fide fishermen. A man might spend the necessary length of time to qualify for the bounty and still not be really engaged in the business. But, if he is a lobster fisherman, you may be pretty sure that he earns his living by fishing. The lobster fishermen have to catch their bait, and when not fishing for lobsters they engage in fishing for cod, mackerel and other fish. Just oue more point. The fishermen will continue to receive their bounties. Hon. gentlemen 'opposite need not worry over that. The bounty has been paid for a good many years, and whatever the regulations may be, the payment will be continued.

It is pleasing to hear the hon. member for King's (Mr. J. J. Hughes) speaking so highly of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. The hon. gentleman has had favours bestowed upon him, and so he [DOT] speaks with feelings My hon.	friend from	East	Prince
(Mr. Lefurgey) and others on this side

have no motive except the welfare of the fishermen, but the hon. member for King's (Mr. J. J. Hughes) may view it with a selfish light, having been benefited as a partner in the fishing business. My hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Le-furgey) asked the Minister of Marine and Fisheries what conclusion had been arrived at with respect to these bounties, and the minister answered that no conclusion had been arrived at. What could my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) conclude but that there had been no move in any direction ? But, as a matter of fact the Minister of Railways, the Finance Minister, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister had an interview with Mr. Peters of Prince Edward Island, and they decided to refer the matter to the Privy Council. My hon. friend (Mr. Pr6-f'ontaine) denies that. I understand that they also decided that, if the Privy Council decided in favour of the provinces, respecting the award, the amount payable to each province shall be decided by arbitration.

I stated that the negotiations were on that line, but that no conclusion had been reached. I have studied the question, because that was part of my duty as Minister of Marine and Fisheries. But before this last interview took place I knew what points would be brought up and discussed. But no decision was arrived at.
But the hon. minister must not forget that his friend from King's (Mr. J. J. Hughes) is quite satisfied as to what the department is going to do.
Because he assumes that we will do what is right.

And my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) is not in the secrets of the minister, and must content himself without even a fair answer to his question. Is that the way the hon. gentleman proposes to admin ister his department ?
I do not understand it that way at all. '

I understand from my hon. friend here that he made a statement which the minister disputed, otherwise he would not have been compelled to quote from the Prince Edward Island paper to substantiate the stand he took.

I do not dispute the statement made by the hon. gentleman. He may make any statement he pleases, 1 am not responsible for it. I only stated what The facts are according to my knowledge, and that is all.
How could the hon. gentleman state that there was no conclusion arrived at ?
Because that is the fact.
He differs from my hon. friend. Does he mean to say that no court has come to a final conclusion ?

I beg my han. friend's pardon. I stated, and I repeat again, rbat negotiations took place, but no conclusion was arrived at with regard to the points upon which we would arbitrate or go before a court, that no conclusion was arrived at one way or the other.
Then this paper was incorrect when it said a decision had been come to to refer the matter to the Privy Council of England 1
No, that was not the statement.
Is it true that this matte is to be referred to the Privy Council in Eng land ?
I have stated jus: now what is true, and nothing else.
Will the minister say that that paper is not correct when it says this matter is to be referred to the Privy Council in England ?
I have given an answer as plain as possible.

Then I say that unless the hon. gentleman contradicts the statement, we must take it as correct. The hon. gentleman in order to support his contention had to quote what the paper stated, but in the first instance the minister did not deny it, he rather affirmed it, I thought ; but now, on second thought, he has denied the statement. Then we have Mr. Peters coming up to Ottawa and then going back to Prince Edward Island, for the purpose of making some political capital, and allowing himself to be interviewed, allowing statements to be made in the public press that are not correct. That is the position, and that is the position the minister evidently bears out in this discussion, that Mr. Peters, according to that interview, has gone back to his province and stated what is not true. If that is the position of affairs, it is first-class literature for the Conservative party in Prince Edward Island.

We cannot understand the facts about this matter unless we have a further statement from the hon member for King's (Mr. Hughes), who seems to be acquainted with it, but will'not tell the committee all he knows. He called on us members from Ontario to say what we thought about it. The first thing we say is that the law should be complied with, that if there is a statute it should be obeyed.
Does the hon. gentleman state that the law has not been complied with ?

I am trying to keep myself right, and I want to see whether the member for King's will put himself right. Now, the minister says, in answer to the member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram), as I understand him, that no conclusion whatever has been arrived at in regard to this matter. I accept that statement. Then no mode indicated by the statute can be suggested to this House at present. The member for King's wishes us to understand that he knows all about this matter, and he is indignant because we ask him to explain a little of what he knows, so that we may vote this money intelligently. When he makes that statement he is in direct conflict with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, to whom he gave such high testimony for his ability and for the wonderful things he has been doing and who says no conclusion has yet been arrived at. He is supporting the minister because he has faith in his ability and fitness,, and believes he will do everything right. That is a pure matter of faith. The member for King's has so much faith in the ability and propriety with which the minister will deal with this matter that he is prepared, without knowing anything about the way he will deal with it, to trust it entirely in his hands. Now, if the minister is correct in saying that no conclusion has been arrived at, then I think the member for King's ought either to ask the minister's permission to put upon the table his own scheme, which he knows all about, or else he ought to correct what he has said to the committee, and say that upon reflection he does not think he ought to ask the Ontario members to vote for an increased expenditure until the statute is complied with. Does the hon. member think that the members for Ontario, to whom he has appealed, ought to vote for an increased expenditure on a certain subject without inquiring how the minister is going to spend that money V I am prepared to vote for any reasonable expenditure when it can be shown that it will be used in the public interest, but I do not like to vote for an expenditure which is likely to be wasted, and unlikely to reach the beneficiaries for whom it is intended-that is the fishermen in this case. The hon. gentleman cannot shirk that question. He cannot ask this committee in all seriousness to say whether it will vote for or against an increase of the expenditure unless he gives it some reasonable ground upon which to exercise its judgment correctly, and those reasonable grounds would be : AVhat mode, as indicated in the statute, is he going to adopt in the payment of the bounty, in order to expend this money so that it" will do some good, and not be wasted politically and in other ways.

I do not wish to retard the passing of this item in the estimates there are one or two matters I desire to refer to. The hon. member for Kings, P.E.I.
(Mr. Hughes) spoke all around the circle because he evidently desired to take a fling at hon. members from Ontario. I am an old member of this parliament. I have been off and on, a member of this parliament for the last quarter of a century, and I have found the members from Ontario as well as the members from the other provinces prepared to do justice to the little province of Prince Edward Island, the smallest province, but still the garden of the gulf. Therefore I say that I have always found the members from Ontario as well as from the other provinces willing to do justice to the province of Prince Edward Island and especially the members on this side of the House. The hon. member for King's talks all around the circle and he ends up by saying that if you pay an additional amount to the lobster fishermen you are paying to the same men ; that is to say that if you are paying $2 to the lobster fishermen and $2 to the deep sea fishermen it all goes to the same men. He suggested to the hon. minister that he should so amend the regulations so as to allow the time spent in the lobster fishery to be included. That is what my hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) is contending for. He contends that the time that the lobster fishermen, who after all is the fisherman of the country, spends in lobster fishing should be counted in the three months which it is necessary to devote to the fishery before he is entitled to the bounty.

There are two qualifications-three months fishing and the taking of 2,500 pounds of deep sea fish. What I meant was that the time spent in fishing for lobsters should count as far as the time is concerned, but that the fishermen should be required to catch 2,500 pounds of deep sea fish. Is that what my hon. friend means ?

My hon. friend has gone back on his proposition. He recommends that the lobster fishermen should receive a share of this bounty but when he finds that lie is cornered he goes back around the circle. Perhaps I am the only man in this House who has had a large experience in reference to the bounty, because for eight or ten years I was the claims officer in Prince Edward Island and I had to go around amongst the fishermen to ascertain their claims in reference to the fishing bounty, i felt that a great grievance existed on the part of the lobster fisherman. He had the necessary quantity of fish. In the herring fishery he would take the full quantity of fish in perhaps two weeks and then he would fish in the lobster fishery for six weeks but when it came to taking the oath that he had fished in the deep sea fishery for the prescribed length of time he could not do it. My hon. friend from East Prince contends that the time spent in the lobster fishery should be included and that the quantity of fish caught in the herring, mackerel or



cod fishery and other branches of the industry should also be included so as to make up the quantity of fish required under the regulations. That is all my hon. friend from East Prince is contending for and my hon. friend from King's will not object to that. It is only a reasonable proposition. It has been said in a way so very characteristic of the hon. Minister of Finance that for so many years this thing has escaped the attention of the government. Well, he has been eight years in office. He says that he represents more lobster fishermen than any other member of this parliament. Now that it has been brought to his notice we ask him to do something and we ask his colleague the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries to come to the relief of the lobster fishermen by allowing him to participate in this bounty as well as those who are supposed to be entitled to it because they are engaged in other branches of the deep sea fishery.
What are these clauses ?
They are as follows :

5. 'Every fishery officer who, by virtue of his appointment as such, is authorized by the Governor in Council, under authority of ' the Fisheries Act,' chapter 95 of the revised statutes, to exercise the powers of a justice of the peace, ex-officio, shall, for all the purposes of this Act and the regulations made under it, be ex-officio a justice of the peace within the district for which he is appointed to act as a fishery officer.
The Governor in Council may, from time to time, make such regulations as he deems necessary or expedient respecting the payment of the said grant and the manner in which applications for the same or any portion thereof shall be made and established, and may require persons applying for the grant or any portion thereof to verify their claims or any statements made by any person in connection therewith, upon oath ; and any such regulations shall, after publication in the 1 Canada Gazette,' have the force of law.
That does not repeal tbe law that we have been talking about.
Don't you be too impatient.
Tbe hon. gentleman stated that he was complying with the law when he has not complied with the law.
Be patient.
We have a good deal of patience and we get very little for it.

55-66 Victoria, chapter 18 passed in 1892 contains the following section.
1.	Section three of an Act to encourage the development of the sea fisheries and the building of fishing vessels, chapter 96 of the revised statutes, is hereby repealed.
So that the obligation of depositing this Order in Council as regards the mode of distributing the bounties is wiped out and we are in the position of having applied the law as it exists. In the statutes of 1882, no mention at all is made of the Halifax award, but it was well understood that the $150,000, which was increased lhter to $160,000, was a kind of compensation for the fishermen whose rights had been infringed on. In the Washington Treaty of 1871, we find that there was no compensation contemplated to be paid for shell fish, shad, salmon, and all fish taken in rivers and in the mouth of rivers. Under the treaty ot 1818, the Americans were excluded from such fisheries, and therefore, it was not contemplated in the Halifax award, that any compensation would be paid by the United States for loss sustained by lobster fishermen, or fishermen who caught shad or salmon, or who fished in the rivers or mouths of rivers ? It is therefore .easy to understand that the question of paying a bounty to the lobster fishermen was not considered at the time. The question comes up now as to whether a bounty should be

paid to lobster fishermen. It is my opinion that those interested in the lobster industry will agree with what the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston) has stated. I am strongly inclined to believe, that the best way to aid lobster fish-men is to furnish them with greater facilities for securing bait, improved modes of preserving the fresh fish, and increased transportation facilities to enable them to put the lobsters fresh upon the market. X think this would have a more beneficial effect, not only on the individual fishermen, but on the industry generally, than would the payment of a paltry sum of one dollar or two dollars to a fisherman. At present we are trying to make the best regulations possible to save the lobster industry from that destruction which has attended it in other countries.) It is 'Only in Canada that we really have a lobster industry. The lobster fishery is depleted in the United States, and they are obliged now to buy their lobsters in Canada for their own market. I do " not claim any particular credit to myself for the efforts which are being made in that department to improve the lobster fishery. When I entered the department eighteen months ago, I knew little about fisheries; I had to work hard to learn, and to take the advice of those who had experience and practical knowledge of all these -questions. In the first place I took the advice given me by my officers, and then I had the views and suggestions of those engaged in the industry to guide me. I may say that the department is supposed to do everything possible to encourage not only the lobster fishermen individually, but the lobster industry in general, so that it may be preserved. Since 1899 we have not only provided bait freezers for ordinary fishermen, but we now intend to provide bait freezers for deep-sea fishermen. On the north coast of Prince Edward Island the cod fishery has been almost abandoned, and it is proposed to bring oflt Scotch fishermen to revive fhfit industry. However, the first) thing to be done is to provide bait freezers. Last year, the suggestion was made to us by some practical fishermen, that we should provide ponds for seed lobsters. This was a new idea, but we adopted it, and I am glad to say that there is reasonable hope to believe the experiment will be a success. Under the present law the fishermen are obliged to return seed lobsters to the water, but as we cannot have an inspector to every trap, we are fairly certain that notwithstanding the care we have exercised for several years past, seed lobsters have been destroyed. When you remember that a seed lobster contains about 10,000 eggs, you will see what a deterrent this must be to the increase of lobsters in our waters. On the suggestion of some practical fisheries
men, we leased a pond, and we set aside a certain amount of money to buy these seed lobsters from the fishermen at about the same price as they would obtain for them if they sold them in the ordinary way. The result was that we deposited in that pond last year over 50,000 seed lobsters, and the report of our inspector is to the effect that millions of small lobsters were put back into the sea, that at least as many young lobsters were put back as were caught in the whole season. In view of the success we have had, we intend to extend this system to other places where we think it is convenient and practicable to do it, and we hope to help in this way, not only the fishing industry, but directly and indirectly the lobster fishermen themselves.

I am very much pleased with the statement made by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Having listened carefully to the discussion on this question I was surprised that none of the hon. gentlemen who had spoken on the subject referred to the propagation of lobsters. That to my mind is the most important thing we can do for the lobster fisheries of the maritime provinces. It is not by paying the fishermen a small bounty that we can increase this industry. To my mind the question is whether we can preserve the industry at all. It has gone down considerably on the coasts of the maritime provinces during recent years. It is also a well-known fact that there was a large lobster industry on the coasts of the United States some years ago. Lobsters were caught on the coasts of New York and Massachusetts, and even as far south as Cape Hatteras. But they have practically disappeared from the coast of the United States except along a E portion of the eoast of the state of Maine. So that, as the minister has said, we have now practically the control of the lobster fisheries of the world, and it is of the utmost importance that we should see that everything possible is done to prevent them disappearing from our coasts as they have done from the coasts of Norway and the other northern countries of Europe, and from the coast of the United States. The efforts of the government should be directed to increasing the number of lobster hatcheries and pounds along the coast of Canada. The work that has been done in this direction on the coast of Pictou county is admitted to have been very successful. I have followed that question for some years past.
I have visited the hatchery year" after year,
I think it is now about eleven years since it was established. For four or five years the fishermen were of opinion that it was a waste of money, and that the young lobsters which wei'e put into the sea never came to anything ; but as time passed on, and it was found that the fishermen on that coast were doing better than the fishermen

on any other part of the coast of Nova Scotia, they began to change their opinions ; and now you will not find a fisherman or a lobster packer within thirty or forty miles of that hatchery who is not of opinion that it has done a great deal to increase the catch in that locality. If we could have lobster hatcheries established along the coasts of the other counties of Nova Scotia where lobsters are caught, they would do a great deal more for the fishermen than the paying of a bounty to them for destroying the lobsters. What we want to do is to preserve and propagate the lobster and that is the direction in which the government should expend money. It is well known that the lobsters have considerably diminished. The fishermen do not catch as many as they did some years ago. I am told that the individual fisherman does not catch half as many in a day as he did fifteen or twenty years ago ; but I am glad to say that he gets for the half that he does catch a better price than he got for the larger quantity he caught formerly. In that way the business has been kept up. I also agree with what my hon. friend from Cape Breton has said in regard to improved transportation. We all know that fish is a perishable commodity, and if we cannot place it in the market quickly, it becomes worthless. The importance of suitable transportation facilities has been illustrated by the great progress that has been made with the halibut industry on the western coast of Canada. That industry did not exist until a few years ago ; but, with the appliances supplied by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Dominion Express Company, it has been worked up, so that now western halibut can be placed on the markets of Boston and New York more quickly and more readily than o'ur halibut caught in the eastern waters. I will read an extract from the ' Pishing Oazette ' :
During the year 1903 there was shipped from Vancouver, B.C., by the Canadian Pacific Railroad 296 car loads of halibut of 24,000 pounds each. These large consignments come principally to New York and Boston, although some of it was landed in Chicago and other western centres. This amount will he undoubtedly exceeded this season. The splendid service given by the railroads, both in time and equipment of refrigerator cars, has been one of the strong factors helping to build up the business, so that to-day the halibut caught on the Pacific coast are not as old when they arrive in Boston or New York as fish caught on the halibut grounds of the east and landed at these points. This is owing to the great distance the vessels are obliged to go in the east and on account of' the scarcity of the fish and the great length of time it takes to catch enough to make it a paying proposition to the vessel and crew.
That progress could not have been made in the halibut industry on the western coast of Canada if railway facilities had not peen supplied. The fast train placed on the Intercolonial Railway a few years ago be-Mr. SINCLAIR.
tween Mulgrave and Montreal has done a great deal to build up the fishing industry on the eastern coast of Nova Scotia. Prior to that date a car of fish was sometimes left on a siding for days, so that when it arrived on the market it was worthless. But now. we can have fish shipped daily at Mulgrave with the knowledge that in fifty-one hours it will arrive in Montreal. We have on the Intercolonial what we never had before* a fast freight train, and it has done more to build up the fishing industry in the east than all the bounties paid by the government. Providing cold storage, giving better railway facilities and propogating the fish- these are the practical ways in which the government can benefit the fresh fish industry in the maritime provinces.

I have listened with some anxiety to the statement made by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to-night. The province of Nova Scotia has been pressing for many years to have the fishery award handed over to the provinces.
Does my hon. friend say that the province of Nova Scotia was pressing for this ?
I understood that Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces wanted the whole sum handed over to them.
I do not think the hon. gentleman has any warrant at all f or that statement.
Then I am entirely misled by the statement of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, because I understood it to involve that question.
No.
What was the question ?

The discussion came up on the question of what were the claims made by the different provinces to a share of the Halifax award. I did not mention the province 'of Nova Scotia at all, but the discussion was more regarding what had been said by Mr. Peters, the premier of Prince Edward Island, than anything else.

It is very astonishing that some gentlemen seem to be startled by an announcement of this kind. The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Alex. Johnston) did not know that any one of the provinces had made a claim for any portion of the award.
I was not in the least startled, but only wanted to point out that the statement which the hon. gentleman made was inaccurate.
Will the hon. gentleman then be good enough to enlighten us as to wlia.t the claims are that are being urged ?
On behalf of Nova Scotia ?
On behalf of the maritime provinces generally.
I have already said that the assertion that the province of Nova Scotia was pressing the matter on the attention of the federal government is inaccurate.

All we can conclude is that the hon. gentleman does not seem to know anything about his own province. We are not surprised that he should resume his seat without being able to give some intelligible information.

Let me say emphatically that Nova Scotia has not asked the government to make any change in the regulations which have existed since the fishery bounties were given to the fishermen in Nova Sc'otia. That province is rather opposed to any change in the existing conditions and does not participate in the agitation from Prince Edward Island ip any manner or form.
and no trade could be done in shipping live lobsters from that part of the coast. The only thing to be done is to continue the hatcheries. While the fish have not yet increased in size, they are increasing in numbers. I would be rather inclined to see the government continue the present system; than divert a portion of the bounty to the lobster fishermen. There is some irregularity about the payment of the bounty. la the county of Pictou, I am Informed that some of those who have received a bounty in some years do not get it in other years. Their application is sometimes refused, and men who have had, the bounty for a number of years find themselves left without it. I have several cases of this kind in mind, which I intend to bring more particularly to the attention of the department. But in the meantime I would be glad if the minister could give me any general explanation how it is that men who have received the bounty for years find themselves excluded for no apparent reas'on. They tell me that their practice is the same and they fish the same number of days, and yet no bounty cheques are sent.

I am glad to learn that, as we were led to believe that all the provinces were urging for some participation in the award. I would like t'o ask the Minister of Marine if the government has consented to re-open the question.

I can only repeat what I have said. There may have been negotiations-that is to say the government could not refuse to hear what those gentlemen had to state-but no conclusion whatever either to open the question or not has been come to ?

Prom what the hon. minister has said I suppose there is no intention on the part of the department to make any change in the regulations as regards the, bounties. He is disposed to abide by the present regulations and assist the lobster fishermen by providing a better supply of bait and greater conveniences for the assembling of the fish ft the factories and, 1 suppose, continuing the lobster hatcheries which we have at present. I know that the subject is exceedingly difficult and complicated. On the south shore it is claimed that the reduction in the number of certain lobsters leads to a l'oss of sea vegetation and the consequent scarcity of other fish, so that the maintenance of the lobster industry is important to other fishing industries on the coast. There is one improvement which it would be very desirable to make, and that is to have some method by which the size of the lobsters on the Nova Scotia coast could be increased. In the western part of the province they catch fairly large fish, which are shipped to the United States alive and bring remunerative prices, but on our coast the large fish are becoming scarce

If my hon. friend will give me particulars of the cases to which he refers I will gladly investigate.. From information I have received from my officials I am led to believe that very few complaints have been made lately. Of course, where there are so many cases to be dealt with there must be some who express dissatisfaction.
How do these cases occur, is it through clerical oversight ?

No, I do not recall any cases of that kind. Sometimes there may be two parties claim. Sometimes the regulations are not fulfilled. All the cases are personally investigated. I repeat, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell) has any special cases, it will be sufficient for him to leave them to the special officer in charge of this business, Mr. Kent, and that officer-will try to do justice in the matter.
I intend to do that, but I thought there might be some general explanation of these cases given by the minister.
There were so few complaints they were not brought to my notice except in special Instances.

I would remind the minister that I brought to the notice of the department a ease which seemed to be a very important one. The master of the vessel had omitted to take the license, and, having taken his departure from the port he requested that the managing owner should make the application and get the license. The request was made only through the clerk in the fishing office of the manag-

iug owner, and the managing owner in consequence, did not know of the omission until a month or so had elapsed from the time the vessel took her departure from port. I recommended that to the department-I do not know that I had an interview with the minister himself-but nevertheless the bounty was not paid, and, in consequence the whole crew were deprived of their portion of the bounty. I hope the minister will carefully reconsider this matter and grant these people the bounty to which, I think, they are fairly entitled. They did not ignore their duty of making application ; it was purely an omissiom When such occurs accidently, I think the minister should treat it as an exceptional case and meet the request of the parties.

speechtext:
I think we have had a very good day's work, and a very fruitful one. We are not likely to make much further progress. If this item is passed we can rise. But, if hon. gentlemen wish to debate it further we can do so.

Of course, Monday is a private members' day. But if the business standing on the order paper in the name of private members is exhausted what government business, if any, will be taken up ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the order of private members' business is exhausted we shall proceed with Supply, beginning at the point at which we have just left off, unless tjhe Minister of Marine and Fisheries is not here in time. But, in that case, the Postmaster General will take up his estimates.
